President, Federated Farmers (2020–2023) | | **Born** | 1974 or 1975 | | **2026 election** | contesting Rangitīkei, list #3 | | **Wikipedia** | [Andrew Hoggard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Hoggard) | Photo: Supplied to policy.nz by the candidate/party — [source](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/ubdwo62y/production/9aaef1deb03bd4e0f6489fd4ea8063c71f309c7a-1024x1024.jpg) ## Current status ACT list MP since 2023 and minister outside Cabinet (Biosecurity; Food Safety; Associate Agriculture and Environment). Standing in **Rangitīkei** and **#3** on ACT's list for 2026. ## Biography Born 1974 or 1975; educated at Heretaunga College, Upper Hutt, and Massey University (Bachelor of Agricultural Economics, 1996). Dairy farmer at Kiwitea, Manawatū, from 1998; Taranaki–Manawatū Young Farmer of the Year (2003). Held Federated Farmers leadership roles from 2014 — dairy chair, vice-president, then president from June 2020 until stepping down early on 8 May 2023 — and sat on the International Dairy Federation board. As president he opposed Labour's planned pricing of agricultural emissions. ## Political career - ACT member since 2019; announced as ACT's Rangitīkei candidate the day after leaving Federated Farmers. Third in Rangitīkei in 2023; elected at list #5. - Minister for Biosecurity and Food Safety and Associate Minister of Agriculture and Environment from November 2023. ## Record & notable actions - Suspended (announced March 2024) councils' obligations to identify new Significant Natural Areas for three years during RMA reform. - Halted poultry exports after an H7N6 avian influenza outbreak near Moeraki (December 2024). - Rewrote pig welfare rules (October 2025): farrowing crates retained with tighter rules and a 10-year transition rather than banned — released papers showed the National Animal Welfare Advisory Committee had disagreed. - Confirmed in March 2026 that the coalition would not reverse the live-animal export ban this term, as Cabinet consensus could not be reached. - Backed investor-funded voluntary carbon and nature markets (May 2026). ## Controversies - **SNA announcement (March 2024):** his statement that the SNA requirement was suspended was described by law professor Andrew Geddis as "misleading at best, and borderline unlawful at worst" because a minister cannot remove a statutory duty by announcement; Hoggard clarified that no legal change had yet taken effect. - **Infant formula standards (2024–25):** his decision not to adopt the joint trans-Tasman infant formula standard was welcomed by industry but criticised by the College of Midwives; RNZ reported he had been lobbied heavily by dairy companies (including through his sister), after which the government reconsidered. ## 2026 candidacy - **Electorate:** Rangitīkei - **List ranking:** 3 - **Before politics:** Dairy Farmer - **Age:** 51 - **Public email:** andrew.hoggard@parliament.govt.nz - **Website:** https://www.act.org.nz/people/andrew-hoggard - **Facebook:** https://www.facebook.com/andrewhoggardact - **Instagram:** https://www.instagram.com/andrewhoggardact - **Twitter:** https://x.com/actparty _Source: candidate questionnaire answers published on [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/act-party), retrieved Oct 2026._ ## Sources - https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Andrew_Hoggard&oldid=1356636423 - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Party_lists_in_the_2026_New_Zealand_general_election - https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/511689/government-drops-need-for-councils-to-comply-with-significant-natural-areas-provisions - https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/556997/how-multinational-dairy-companies-convinced-ministers-to-back-away-from-new-rules-for-baby-formula - https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/in-depth/576140/govt-s-independent-animal-welfare-experts-disagreed-with-pig-welfare-reforms - https://www.1news.co.nz/2026/03/10/will-be-disappointment-live-export-ban-wont-be-overturned-this-term/ - https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/country/535456/all-poultry-exports-on-hold-until-nz-free-of-highly-pathogenic-bird-flu - https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/act-party

# Brooke van Velden | | | |---|---| | **Party (current/most recent)** | ACT New Zealand | | **Status** | MP (54th Parliament), retiring at 2026 election | | **Party history** | ACT New Zealand (c. 2014–present) | | **Parliaments (50th–54th)** | 53, 54 | | **First elected** | 2020 | | **Electorates held** | Tāmaki (2023–2026) | | **Key roles** | Minister of Internal Affairs (2023–)

Deputy Leader of ACT (2020–2026)
ACT whip (2020–2023) | | **Born** | 1992-10-15, Auckland | | **Wikipedia** | [Brooke van Velden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooke_van_Velden) | Photo: Health & Safety Association NZ — CC BY 4.0 — [source](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Brooke_van_Velden_at_2024_HASANZ_Conference_(cropped).jpg) ## Current status MP for Tāmaki and a Cabinet minister (Internal Affairs; Workplace Relations and Safety) in the National–ACT–NZ First government. **Retiring** at the 2026 election (announced 24 March 2026); replaced as ACT deputy leader by Nicole McKee on 28 June 2026. ## Biography Born in Auckland on 15 October 1992 to a nurse and a mechanic who later ran car-sales businesses; educated at St Cuthbert's College and the University of Auckland (BA/BCom in economics and international trade, 2016). Worked for lobbying firm Exceltium, then as a staffer for David Seymour, spending two years lobbying MPs and helping draft the End of Life Choice Bill. Says she was a Green voter before switching to ACT at university. ## Political career - ACT candidate for Auckland Central in 2017 (list #3, not elected). - Elected ACT deputy leader in June 2020 aged 27; entered Parliament on the list in 2020 (ACT whip; health, housing, foreign affairs and trade spokesperson). - Won **Tāmaki** in 2023 by 4,158 votes, ending National's hold since 1960. - Became one of the youngest Cabinet ministers in New Zealand history in November 2023. ## Record & notable actions - Repealed Labour's Fair Pay Agreements Act (December 2023). - Set minimum wage increases (2% to $23.15 in April 2024); expanded the terms of reference of the Royal Commission into COVID-19 lessons. - **Equal Pay Amendment Act 2025**: passed under urgency on 6–7 May 2025, raising thresholds for pay-equity claims and stopping 33 existing claims; strongly opposed by unions and opposition parties. - **Employment Relations Amendment Act 2026** (passed 17 February 2026): "gateway test" for contractors, tighter personal-grievance rules, no remedies for dismissals for serious misconduct, removal of the 30-day rule. - Holidays Act overhaul toward hours-based accrual of leave; online casino licensing bill (2025); a citizenship test from mid-2027. - WorkSafe "road cone tipline" (June–December 2025), shut down after ~1,300 notifications at a cost of about $150,000. - Moved the 2021 parliamentary motion on human-rights abuses against Uyghurs in Xinjiang (adopted unanimously after Labour removed the word "genocide"). ## Controversies - The pay-equity changes were a major controversy; a Labour branch's Facebook post depicting her in a Nazi uniform was deleted and Labour's leadership apologised. In a May 2025 debate she quoted an expletive from a Stuff column criticising her, drawing criticism from Winston Peters. - A 2023 comment that during COVID New Zealand "completely blew out what the value of a life was" was criticised by opponents. ## Sources - https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Brooke_van_Velden&oldid=1380177812 - https://newsroom.co.nz/2026/03/24/van-velden-to-step-down/ - https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/members-of-parliament/van-velden-brooke/ - https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/health/euthanasia-debate/117370430/formidable-brooke-van-velden-the-end-of-life-choice-bill-lobbyist-youve-probably-never-heard-of - https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/125034356/parliament-unanimously-declares-severe-human-rights-abuses-occurring-against-uyghur-in-china - https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2025/0024/latest/whole.html

# David Seymour | | | |---|---| | **Party (current/most recent)** | ACT New Zealand | | **Status** | MP (54th Parliament), standing in 2026 | | **Party history** | ACT New Zealand (early 2000s–present) | | **Parliaments (50th–54th)** | 51, 52, 53, 54 | | **First elected** | 2014 | | **Electorates held** | Epsom (2014–) | | **Key roles** | Leader of ACT (2014–)
Deputy Prime Minister (2025–)
Minister for Regulation (2023–)
Associate Minister of Education (partnership schools), Finance and Health (Pharmac) (2023–)
Acting Prime Minister (14–20 July 2024)
Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Education and Regulatory Reform (2014–2017) | | **Born** | 1983-06-24, Palmerston North | | **2026 election** | contesting Epsom, list #1 | | **Wikipedia** | [David Seymour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Seymour) | Photo: Supplied to policy.nz by the candidate/party — [source](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/ubdwo62y/production/db78c5fc5a012f843362a4f0cb4e8798f93ac5f8-1024x1024.jpg) ## Current status Leader of ACT, MP for Epsom since 2014, **Deputy Prime Minister** since 31 May 2025 (under the coalition's job-share with Winston Peters) and the first **Minister for Regulation**. Standing again in **Epsom** and **#1** on ACT's list for 7 November 2026. ## Biography Born in Palmerston North on 24 June 1983 and raised in Whangārei; has Ngāpuhi (Ngāti Rēhia) ancestry through a great-great-great-grandmother. Educated at Auckland Grammar and the University of Auckland (BE in electrical and electronic engineering and BA in philosophy, 2006). Worked in engineering and then for about five years as a policy analyst at Canadian conservative think tanks (Frontier Centre for Public Policy, Manning Centre) and completed the Atlas Network's 2008 "MBA for Think Tanks" programme. Former president of ACT on Campus. Contestant on *Dancing with the Stars* (2018). ## Political career - ACT candidate in Mt Albert (2005), list-only (2008) and Auckland Central (2011). - Adviser to ACT leader John Banks (2011–2014), working on the partnership schools legislation. - Won **Epsom** in 2014 (with John Key's tacit endorsement) as ACT's sole MP and became leader on 3 October 2014; Parliamentary Under-Secretary for Education and Regulatory Reform 2014–2017. - Sole ACT MP again in 2017; led ACT to 10 seats in 2020 and a record 11 seats (8.64%) in 2023, after which ACT joined the National-led coalition. ## Record & notable actions - **End of Life Choice Act 2019**: his member's bill legalising assisted dying passed its third reading 69–51 with a referendum requirement added for NZ First; approved by 65.9% in the 2020 referendum. - **Regulatory Standards Act**: as Minister for Regulation sponsored the Regulatory Standards Bill (passed third reading along party lines on 13 November 2025), setting principles for good law-making emphasising individual and property rights; criticised by legal academics such as Jane Kelsey. - **Treaty Principles Bill**: ACT's bill redefining the principles of the Treaty of Waitangi was supported to select committee under the coalition deal but defeated at second reading 11–112 on 10 April 2025; it prompted the Hīkoi mō te Tiriti, one of the largest protests in New Zealand history. - As Associate Education Minister reintroduced charter (partnership) schools ($153 million in Budget 2024 for 35 conversions and 15 new schools) and redesigned the free school lunch programme (Ka Ora, Ka Ako) to a cheaper bulk-supplied model — whose 2025 rollout drew complaints about food quality. - As Associate Health Minister restored over-the-counter pseudoephedrine sales (2024) and directed Pharmac to stop factoring the Treaty of Waitangi into decisions. - The only MP to vote against the 2019 semi-automatic firearms ban (119–1); removed "safe zones" from the 2020 abortion law (later reinstated with his support in 2022); passed a 2015 bill allowing early-morning bar openings for the Rugby World Cup. ## Controversies - **Māori and co-governance:** a vocal opponent of co-governance, He Puapua and the Māori Health Authority; critics including Te Pāti Māori, Labour's Willie Jackson and many iwi leaders accuse him of divisive, majoritarian politics, while supporters see a defence of equal citizenship. - **Māori vaccination code (2021):** publicly tweeted a booking access code intended for Māori at a Whānau Waipareira vaccination site; criticised by CEO John Tamihere and others. - **"Guy Fawkes" remark (2023):** joked on Newstalk ZB about sending "a guy like Guy Fawkes" into the Ministry for Pacific Peoples; condemned by PM Chris Hipkins and others; # John Banks | | | |---|---| | **Party (current/most recent)** | ACT New Zealand | | **Status** | Former MP | | **Party history** | National (1970s–c. 2011); ACT New Zealand (2011-05-18–2014) | | **Parliaments (50th–54th)** | 50 | | **First elected** | 1981 | | **Electorates held** | Whangarei (1981–1999, National), Epsom (2011–2014, ACT) | | **Key roles** | Leader of ACT (2012–2014)
Minister for Regulatory Reform and Minister for Small Business (2011–2013)
Associate Minister of Commerce and of Education (2011–2013)
Minister of Police, Tourism and Sport (1990–1994/96)
Mayor of Auckland City (2001–2004, 2007–2010) | | **Born** | 1946-12-02, Wellington | | **Wikipedia** | [John Banks (New Zealand politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Banks_(New_Zealand_politician)) | Photo: Governor-General of New Zealand — CC BY-SA 4.0 — [source](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:John_Banks.jpg) ## Current status Former MP and former ACT leader. Resigned from Parliament in June 2014 after a High Court conviction for filing a false electoral return, which was later overturned; in May 2015 the Court of Appeal declined to order a retrial after new evidence showed Kim and Mona Dotcom's account had been fabricated. Not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Born in Wellington on 2 December 1946; his parents were imprisoned for procuring abortions when he was a child and from age two he was raised by an aunt and uncle among many foster children, later attending Avondale College. Worked in pharmaceutical market research, commercial property development and restaurants. Birkenhead Borough councillor from 1977. Married Amanda Medcalf in 1987 (later separated); they adopted three children from St Petersburg. CNZM (2011), QSO (2000). A long-time talkback host (Radio Pacific 1992–2007; later MagicTalk). ## Political career - National MP for Whangarei 1981–1999; Minister of Police, Tourism and Sport from 1990; left Cabinet in 1996 rather than serve alongside coalition partner Winston Peters; retired in 1999. - Mayor of Auckland City 2001–2004 (lost to Dick Hubbard) and 2007–2010; lost the 2010 Auckland "super city" mayoralty to Len Brown. - Joined ACT in May 2011 and won **Epsom** in 2011 (after the "cup of tea" with John Key) as ACT's only MP; ACT leader from February 2012 to 2014 (succeeded by Jamie Whyte, who was not an MP). Minister outside Cabinet in John Key's government until resigning his portfolios in October 2013 when committed for trial. ## Record & notable actions - As a 1990s minister he said he could not persuade Cabinet to ban semi-automatic guns after Aramoana; after the 2019 Christchurch attacks he said he was "haunted" by that. - As ACT leader secured, under the 2011 confidence-and-supply deal, the introduction of partnership (charter) schools. - Voted for the 2013 marriage equality law, saying that "if I knew then what I have since learnt, I would have acted differently" — reversing his 1986 opposition to homosexual law reform. - The Local Electoral Amendment Act 2013 (the "John Banks bill") tightened rules on anonymous local-election donations in response to his 2010 return. ## Controversies - **False electoral return (2010–2015):** charged by private prosecution over two $25,000 donations from Kim Dotcom declared as anonymous; convicted on 1 August 2014 (two months' community detention), conviction quashed on appeal in November 2014, and no retrial ordered in May 2015. - Long record of contentious remarks: opposing 1986 homosexual law reform ("sad and sickening day"), comments about Asian immigrants (2004) and Māori men in a safe-sex campaign (2006); in January 2021 MagicTalk dropped him after he agreed on air with a caller that Māori were a "stone age" people. - The 2011 "teapot tape" — a journalist's recording of his private conversation with John Key — became a major election-campaign controversy. - In a 2016 paternity case brought by Antony Shaw, the High Court declared Banks to be Shaw's birth father; Shaw's mother alleged in an affidavit that Banks had pressured her to take drugs to induce a miscarriage in 1969, which Banks had denied. ## Sources - https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=John_Banks_(New_Zealand_politician)&oldid=1347319196 - http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11268295 - http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11393301 - https://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA1304/S00335/speech-john-banks-on-voting-for-marriage-amendment-bill.htm - https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/christchurch-shooting/111644333/haunted-john-banks-says-semiautomatic-weapons-should-have-been-banned-in-1990 - http://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2013/0040/27.0/DLM4803506.html

Standing in **North Shore** and **#5** on ACT's list for 2026. ## Biography Of Ngāpuhi descent; born in Australia and raised by grandparents in Kaeo before returning to her mother on Auckland's North Shore at five. She ran away from home repeatedly as a child and spent time in state/foster care, which she cites as the reason for her focus on child welfare. Worked in property management before politics. ## Political career - Contested Upper Harbour in 2020 and 2023 (fourth both times); elected at list #7 in 2020 and re-elected in 2023. - Minister for Children and Minister for the Prevention of Family and Sexual Violence from November 2023. ## Record & notable actions - **Repeal of section 7AA of the Oranga Tamariki Act** (Treaty obligations/whānau placement): she introduced a member's bill in 2022 and, as minister, the government bill passed its third reading on 3 April 2025. She argued the clause meant "children being put second"; the Waitangi Tribunal's interim report said the repeal would harm vulnerable children. - **Waitangi Tribunal summons (2024)**: the Tribunal summonsed her to give evidence; the High Court set aside the summons, but the Court of Appeal reinstated it on 13 May 2024, the day the repeal bill was introduced (which ended the inquiry). - Launched a military-style academy pilot for serious youth offenders (July 2024), criticised by the Greens, Te Pāti Māori, IHC and academics; introduced a Youth Serious Offender declaration and expanded monitoring powers. - Created an independent Child Protection Investigation Unit (November 2024). - Opposed Labour's Smokefree generational tobacco ban as unworkable (2021). ## Controversies - In September 2022 Children's Minister Kelvin Davis told her to "enter the Māori world" and stop looking through a "vanilla lens"; he apologised the next day. - In 2024 she said she faced bullying and an "unsafe work environment" at Parliament after Te Pāti Māori posts linked her views to her uplifting as a child and MP Mariameno Kapa-Kingi called her an ACT "puppet"; Announced in December 2022 that she would not stand in 2023, and left Parliament at that election. Not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Born in Auckland in 1958 and educated at St Cuthbert's College and the University of Auckland (arts and law). She worked as a communications officer for the New Zealand Forest Service on the West Coast, then from 1984 to 1990 at Parliament as a Labour research officer and press secretary to Helen Clark. After moving to Christchurch she was a freelance journalist and, from 1993 to 2007, a field officer and spokesperson for Forest & Bird, campaigning on the environmental impacts of logging, mining and dairying. the elected council was replaced by government-appointed commissioners in 2010, which she said prompted her to run for Parliament. - Green list MP 2011–2023 (contested Selwyn 2011, Port Hills 2014 and 2017, Banks Peninsula 2020). - In the first term of the Sixth Labour Government (2017–2020) she was Minister of Conservation, Minister for Land Information and Associate Minister for the Environment (Greens' ministers outside Cabinet under the confidence-and-supply deal). - Chair of Parliament's Environment Committee 2020–2023. ## Record & notable actions - Led development of Te Mana o te Taiao, the Aotearoa New Zealand Biodiversity Strategy; after criticism (including from the Law Society) Labour removed it and the Greens withdrew support for the bill. - Voted for marriage equality (2013), the End of Life Choice Act (2019) and the Abortion Legislation Act (2020). ## Controversies - Her Himalayan tahr cull plan (2019–20) drew strong opposition from hunters, led to death threats against her, and was scaled back. - As Land Information Minister she was criticised by former Green MP Sue Bradford for approving "nearly every" overseas land-purchase application despite Green policy; She attributed her actions to "an extreme stress response" linked to previously unrecognised trauma, and apologised. - **Tribunal defence work:** in 2017 it emerged she had worked as an intern on defence teams for accused war criminals including Radovan Karadžić and Simon Bikindi; she said fair trials required defence counsel and she would "do it again". - **Comments on Israel–Palestine:** in 2019 she apologised after the NZ Jewish Council said a tweet calling Mary and Joseph "Palestinian refugees" denied Jewish connection to the land; in 2021 the Council criticised her comments on the Sheikh Jarrah dispute. - In 2019 ACT leader David Seymour called her "a menace to freedom" over her views on hate speech, comparing such views to tactics of Mao, Stalin and Hitler; the comments were widely criticised across Parliament. ## Sources - https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Golriz_Ghahraman&oldid=1378171647 - https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/former-members-of-parliament/ghahraman-golriz/ - https://www.theguardian.com/world/2017/oct/07/new-zealand-election-full-results-labour-boost-and-first-refugee-mp - https://www.newsroom.co.nz/2017/11/27/63852/the-green-mp-and-the-genocide-hearings - https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/133563837/golriz-ghahraman-resigns-amid-shoplifting-accusations - https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/350210512/former-green-mp-golriz-ghahraman-pleads-guilty-shoplifting - https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/new-zealand/2024/06/former-green-party-mp-golriz-ghahraman-gets-1600-fine-for-shoplifting.html

# James Shaw | | | |---|---| | **Party (current/most recent)** | Green Party | | **Status** | Former MP | | **Party history** | Green Party (1990s–present) | | **Parliaments (50th–54th)** | 51, 52, 53, 54 | | **First elected** | 2014 | | **Key roles** | Green Party co-leader (2015–2024)

Associate Minister for the Environment (Biodiversity) (2020–2023) | | **Born** | 1973-05-06, Wellington | | **Wikipedia** | [James Shaw (New Zealand politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Shaw_(New_Zealand_politician)) | Photo: Supplied by the Green Party; uploader will deal with VRT — CC BY-SA 4.0 — [source](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:James_Shaw_2023_%28cropped%29.jpg) ## Current status Former MP and former Green co-leader. Stepped down as co-leader in March 2024 (succeeded by Chlöe Swarbrick) and left Parliament on 5 May 2024 (replaced by Francisco Hernandez). Now works in climate-related business and governance roles, including Morrison & Co. Not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Born in Wellington on 6 May 1973 and raised mainly by his mother Cynthia Shaw and later also her partner Susanne Jungersen. Attended Wellington High School and Victoria University of Wellington, then spent 12 years in London, where he completed an MSc in sustainability and business leadership at the University of Bath (2005) and worked in PwC's consulting division. Returned to Wellington in 2010 and worked for HSBC on environmental-leadership programmes and at the Akina Foundation social enterprise. Married to Annabel; lives in Aro Valley. ## Political career - Volunteered for the Greens from 1990; stood for Wellington City Council at 19 (1992). - Green candidate in Wellington Central 2011, 2014, 2017 and 2020; list MP from 2014. - Elected male co-leader on 30 May 2015 after seven months as an MP, beating Kevin Hague (54% to 44% of first preferences). Sole leader through the 2017 campaign after Metiria Turei's resignation; co-leader with Marama Davidson from 2018. - Minister for Climate Change, Minister of Statistics and Associate Minister of Finance (outside Cabinet) from 2017 under the Labour–NZ First–Green arrangement; retained Climate Change and gained Associate Environment (Biodiversity) under the 2020 cooperation agreement. - Re-elected co-leader 116–4 against James Cockle (2021). Not reconfirmed in the July 2022 annual vote, triggering a contest; re-elected with 142 of 145 delegate votes (97%) on 10 September 2022. - Announced in January 2024 he would step down as co-leader; his Bill of Rights amendment adding a "right to a sustainable environment" was defeated at first reading on 10 April 2024. ## Record & notable actions - **Climate Change Response (Zero Carbon) Amendment Act 2019**: introduced by Shaw in May 2019, it set net-zero targets for long-lived gases by 2050, created the independent Climate Change Commission and a system of emissions budgets. It passed with near-unanimous support. - Backed the 2018 decision to end new offshore oil and gas exploration permits ("nuclear-free moment of our generation"). - Represented New Zealand at UN climate conferences (COP) during 2017–2023. - Described himself as part of a "pro-market" Green tradition that believes markets can be reformed to incorporate sustainability. ## Controversies - **Green School funding (2020):** approved $11.7 million from the COVID-19 "shovel-ready" fund for a private school in Taranaki, contrary to Green policy against state funding of private schools; criticised by teachers' unions, principals and former Green MPs. He apologised on 1 September 2020 calling it "an error of judgment"; the grant was later converted into a loan. Education Minister Chris Hipkins disputed Shaw's account that he had given verbal approval. - **2018 census**: as Statistics Minister he was criticised over the census's low response rate. - Criticised in 2018 for the highest ministerial international airfare spending in one quarter (NZ$77,771), which he attributed to climate conferences; and in 2021 for MIQ places allocated to his COP26 delegation. - On 14 March 2019 he was assaulted while walking to Parliament; a 47-year-old man was charged. (Shaw was the victim.) ## Sources - https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=James_Shaw_(New_Zealand_politician)&oldid=1359183916 - https://www.beehive.govt.nz/minister/biography/james-shaw - https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/members-of-parliament/shaw-james/ - http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11457327 - https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/515700/james-shaw-s-valedictory-and-his-new-roles - https://www.legislation.govt.nz/act/public/2019/0061/latest/whole.html

Not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Darleen Sheree Tana Hoff-Nielsen was born in Northland and is of Ngāpuhi, Ngāti Porou, Ngā Rauru, Te Āti Awa and Ngāti Kahungunu ki Wairarapa descent. Educated at Bay of Islands College and Whangārei Girls' High School; Bachelor of Chemical Technology (Massey) and, on a Rotary scholarship, an MBA from Solvay Business School in Brussels, where she worked in telecommunications talent management. Tana denied exploiting workers and said natural justice had not been followed. # Andrew Little | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1965-05-07 — New Plymouth, New Zealand | | **Parliaments** | 50, 51, 52, 53 | | **First elected** | 2011 | | **Key roles** | 38th Mayor of Wellington (2025–)
35th Leader of the Opposition and 16th Leader of the Labour Party (2014–2017)
6th Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations (2017–2023)
42nd Minister of Health (2020–2023)
49th Minister of Justice (2017–2020)
33rd President of the Labour Party (2009–2011) | | **Wikipedia** | [Andrew Little (New Zealand politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Little_%28New_Zealand_politician%29) | ## Current status Little won the October 2025 Wellington mayoral election as Labour's endorsed candidate after incumbent Tory Whanau withdrew and endorsed him ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/559306/andrew-little-secures-labour-mayoral-nomination); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/360851504/mayor-andrew-little-be-joined-wellington-city-council-ray-chung-no-place-tory-whanau)). As mayor he led a review and, in June 2026, a council vote to discontinue the $139m Golden Mile pedestrianisation project ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/598585/councillors-vote-against-continuing-wellington-s-golden-mile-project)), called for an inquiry into the Moa Point sewage plant failure, and declared a local state of emergency for heavy swells in June 2026. He resigned from Parliament on 5 December 2023 (Camilla Belich took his list seat) and is not a 2026 parliamentary candidate. He has publicly supported New Zealand's engagement with AUKUS, unlike Labour's current position ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/524955/former-defence-minister-andrew-little-disagrees-with-aukus-critics-on-china-threat)). ## Biography Born 7 May 1965 in New Plymouth, Little studied law, philosophy and public policy at Victoria University of Wellington and was VUWSA president (1987) and NZUSA president (1988–89). He became a lawyer for the Engineers' Union, its general counsel (1997) and national secretary of the EPMU, New Zealand's largest private-sector union, from 2000 to 2011; he was Labour Party president from 2009 to 2011 ([RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/259657/little-takes-union-path-to-leadership)). He was successfully treated for prostate cancer in 2009 and lives in Island Bay with his wife Leigh and their son. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 50th | 2011–2014 | List | 15 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | List | 11 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 3 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | List | 7 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 38th Mayor of Wellington | 17 October 2025 | present | | | 35th Leader of the Opposition and 16th Leader of the Labour Party | 18 November 2014 | 1 August 2017 | John Key; Bill English | | 6th Minister for Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 42nd Minister of Health | 6 November 2020 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 49th Minister of Justice | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 33rd President of the Labour Party | 2 March 2009 | 2 April 2011 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **List MP, 2011–2023.** Stood unsuccessfully in New Plymouth in 2011 and 2014; list-only thereafter. - **Labour leader and Leader of the Opposition, 18 Nov 2014 – 1 Aug 2017.** Narrowly beat Grant Robertson in the 2014 leadership election, carried by the union affiliates' vote ([Stuff](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/63305825/Andrew-Little-new-Labour-Party-leader-by-a-whisker)). Credited with ending caucus infighting but polled poorly; he resigned seven weeks before the 2017 election, handing over to Jacinda Ardern — a move later widely described as selfless ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11935044)). - **Minister, 2017–2023 (12 portfolios):** Justice and Courts (2017–2020), Treaty of Waitangi Negotiations (2017–2023), GCSB and NZSIS (2017–2023), Pike River Re-entry, Workplace Relations (2020), Health (Nov 2020 – Jan 2023), Defence and Public Service (2023), Immigration (June 2023), and lead coordination minister for the Christchurch mosque attack Royal Commission response ([Parliament profile](https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/former-members-of-parliament/little-andrew/)). ## Record & notable actions - **Abortion law reform:** as Justice Minister he introduced the bill that removed abortion from the Crimes Act; it passed as the Abortion Legislation Act 2020 ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/120389800/new-zealands-fourdecade-old-abortion-laws-have-changed-after-law-passes-final-reading)). - **Pike River:** established the Pike River Recovery Agency and in 2018 entered the portal with families; the drift was re-entered in 2019, but plans to recover the miners' remains were abandoned in 2021 ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/andrew-little-enters-pike-river-portal)). - **Health:** as Health Minister (2020–2023) he oversaw the health system through the COVID-19 period; in mid-2022 he said the system was under pressure but not in crisis, which health workers disputed ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/469518/health-system-under-pressure-not-in-crisis-minister-andrew-little)). - **Three strikes:** his 2018 plan to repeal the three-strikes law was blocked by NZ First ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12068425)). - **Intelligence:** in July 2021 publicly attributed malicious cyber activity to Chinese state-sponsored actor APT40 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/447239/government-points-finger-at-china-over-cyber-attacks)). - **Treaty settlements:** delivered Crown apologies including to Ngāti Maru (Taranaki) in 2022. - **Opposition:** drafted a corporate manslaughter member's bill after Pike River and the CTV collapse (2013). ## Controversies - **Defamation suits:** ACC Minister Judith Collins sued Little and Trevor Mallard for defamation in 2012 (settled); in 2017 hotel owners Earl and Lani Hagaman sued him over remarks linking their National Party donation to a government contract — the jury cleared him on some claims and could not agree on others, and no damages were awarded ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10847321); [RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/national/328552/little-%27very-pleased%27-no-damages-awarded)). - **Australian deportations (2018):** a public dispute with Australian ministers Peter Dutton and Alex Hawke after he criticised Australia's "501" deportation policy ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12092448)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - 3rd Minister for Auckland (2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Carmel Sepuloni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmel_Sepuloni) | ## Current status Sepuloni has been Labour's deputy leader since 7 November 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/501872/labour-votes-to-keep-chris-hipkins-as-leader-carmel-sepuloni-takes-over-as-deputy)) and is No. 2 on Labour's 2026 list, contesting the Glendene electorate ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)). Since the March 2025 reshuffle her portfolios have been Pacific Peoples, Auckland Issues and Women; she gave up social development and child poverty reduction ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/544048/chris-hipkins-announces-new-labour-economic-team-tangi-utikere-promoted)). ## Biography Born in 1977 and raised in Waitara, Taranaki, Sepuloni is of Samoan, Tongan and Pākehā descent — her father was a migrant freezing worker and unionist — and she was New Zealand's first MP of Tongan descent ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131030608/who-is-the-new-deputy-prime-minister-carmel-sepuloni); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/national/programmes/morningreport/audio/2018874642/carmel-sepuloni-makes-history-as-first-pasifika-deputy-pm)). She trained as a primary teacher (Auckland College of Education; BEd, University of Auckland; PGDipEd), taught in Samoa and in alternative education in Auckland, and worked in Pacific health research at the University of Auckland. Between her two stints in Parliament she was chief executive of Vaka Tautua, a Pacific disability, mental-health and social-services provider ([Beehive biography](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/minister/biography/carmel-sepuloni)). She has two sons and married writer and musician Daren Kamali in 2018. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | List | 35 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Kelston | 29 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Kelston | 8 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Kelston | 8 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | Kelston | 3 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | Deputy Leader of the Opposition | 27 November 2023 | present | | | 19th Deputy Leader of the Labour Party | 7 November 2023 | present | | | 20th Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand | 25 January 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 5th Minister for Workplace Relations and Safety | 21 June 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 3rd Minister for Auckland | 21 June 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 27th Minister for Social Development | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 14th Minister for ACC | 22 July 2020 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 13th Minister for Arts, Culture and Heritage | 6 November 2020 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 2 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Deputy Leader of the Opposition - Spokesperson for Auckland Issues - Spokesperson for Pacific Peoples - Spokesperson for Women _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ ### Career summary - **List MP, 2008–2011.** Entered at list position 35; civil defence spokesperson. Her Employment Relations (Probationary Period Repeal) Amendment Bill, to repeal the 90-day trial period, was defeated 64–57 at first reading in 2010 ([Scoop](http://business.scoop.co.nz/2010/08/05/member%E2%80%99s-bill-to-remove-90-days-voted-down/)). - **2011 Waitakere loss.** On official results she beat Paula Bennett by 11 votes, but a judicial recount gave Bennett a 9-vote majority and Sepuloni left Parliament ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10773368)). - **Kelston, 2014–present.** Majorities of 15,091 (2014), 16,789 (2017), 15,660 (2020) and 4,396 (2023) ([2014](http://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-21.html), [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-19.html), [2023](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-19.html)). - **Minister, 2017–2023.** Minister for Social Development throughout the Sixth Labour Government; also Disability Issues (2017–2022), ACC (2020–2023), Employment, Arts, Culture and Heritage (2020–2023), and, under Hipkins, Associate Foreign Affairs (Pacific), Workplace Relations and Safety and Minister for Auckland (from June 2023) ([DPMC 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf); [NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/prime-minister-chris-hipkins-reveals-michael-woods-future/EFRLIOY63FE3BCFXFTXFX3OXGQ/)). - **Deputy Prime Minister, 25 Jan – 27 Nov 2023** — the first Pasifika person and third woman in the role ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/01/22/the-girl-from-waitara-carmel-sepuloni-makes-history/)). ## Record & notable actions - As social development minister she led the government's welfare overhaul, which she likened to "trying to turn a jumbo jet in mid-air" ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/shows/2018/04/welfare-overhaul-to-get-underway-in-next-three-years-carmel-sepuloni.html)); main benefits were increased during her tenure (see [Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2020/04/25-benefit-increase-making-a-difference-for-beneficiaries-during-lockdown-carmel-sepuloni.html)). - Represented New Zealand alongside National's Gerry Brownlee at the November 2023 Pacific Islands Forum during the caretaker period ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/11/pacific-islands-forum-carmel-sepuloni-gerry-brownlee-arrive-in-rarotonga.html)). ## Controversies - In 2015 she was temporarily stood down as social development spokesperson after her mother was charged with benefit fraud; her mother was later sentenced to home detention for receiving about $34,000 in benefits illegally. No wrongdoing by Sepuloni was alleged ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/270065/sepuloni%27s-mother-sentenced-for-benefit-fraud)). ## 2026 candidacy - **Electorate:** Glendene - **List ranking:** 2 _Source: candidate questionnaire answers published on [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party), retrieved Oct 2026._ ## Sources - # Chris Hipkins | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Current MP, standing in 2026 | | **Born** | 1978-09-05 — Hutt Valley, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | Rimutaka, Remutaka | | **Parliaments** | 49, 50, 51, 52, 53, 54 | | **First elected** | 2008 | | **2026 candidacy** | Remutaka · list #1 | | **Key roles** | Labour shadow cabinet #1 (as of 11 Mar 2026): Leader of the Opposition; Spokesperson for Ministerial Services; Spokesperson for National Security and Intelligence
41st Leader of the Opposition (2023–)
41st Prime Minister of New Zealand (2023)
18th Leader of the Labour Party (2023–)
Minister of National Security and Intelligence (2023)
Leader of the House (2017–2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Hipkins) | ## Current status Hipkins is Leader of the Opposition and Labour leader heading into the 7 November 2026 general election, in which he is standing again in Remutaka and is first on Labour's list ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)). Labour's caucus confirmed him as leader after the 2023 defeat on 7 November 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/501872/labour-votes-to-keep-chris-hipkins-as-leader-carmel-sepuloni-takes-over-as-deputy)). In October 2025 he announced that Labour would campaign on a narrow 28% capital gains tax on property sales (excluding the family home and farms) to fund three free doctor's visits a year, and ruled out a wealth tax ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/577021/labour-to-campaign-on-narrow-capital-gains-tax-no-wealth-tax)). ## Biography Christopher John Hipkins was born on 5 September 1978 in the Hutt Valley, the son of Doug and Rosemary Hipkins ([Parliament maiden statement](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/document/49HansS_20081216_00001004/hipkins-chris-maiden-statements); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/482831/chris-hipkins-from-head-boy-to-prime-minister)). He was head boy of Hutt Valley Memorial College in 1996 and studied political science and criminology at Victoria University of Wellington (BA), where he was students' association president in 2000 and 2001 ([Beehive biography](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/minister/biography/chris-hipkins)). As a first-year student in 1997 he was among protesters arrested at Parliament over the Tertiary Review green paper; a decade later the protesters received an apology and compensation after a court found the arrests unjustified ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/dominion-post/news/local-papers/hutt-news/2595536/Parliament-to-say-sorry-to-protestors)). Before entering Parliament he was a policy adviser at the Industry Training Federation, a training manager at Todd Energy, and an adviser to ministers Trevor Mallard and Prime Minister Helen Clark ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/chris-hipkins-from-hutt-valley-boy-to-quiet-coup-for-pm-audrey-young-reports/ET4JZSI5PVCKBDDHRCLYVQ3CHI/)). He married Jade in 2020; they separated in 2022 and have two children. In 2018 he took extended paternity leave, one of the first senior male cabinet ministers to do so. His relationship with Toni Grace became public on election night 2023 and he announced their engagement in November 2025 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-leader-chris-hipkins-reveals-engagement-to-partner-toni-grace/32RDT6TDINBDBCJ3XR2Z23OIAQ/)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | Rimutaka | 47 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | Rimutaka | 30 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Rimutaka | 9 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Rimutaka | 7 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Remutaka | 6 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | Remutaka | 1 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 41st Leader of the Opposition | 27 November 2023 | present | Christopher Luxon | | 41st Prime Minister of New Zealand | 25 January 2023 | 27 November 2023 | | | 18th Leader of the Labour Party | 22 January 2023 | present | | | Minister of National Security and Intelligence | 25 January 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Himself | | Leader of the House | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Education | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Public Service | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Police | 14 June 2022 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister for COVID-19 Response | 6 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister of Health | 2 July 2020 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 1 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Leader of the Opposition - Spokesperson for Ministerial Services - Spokesperson for National Security and Intelligence _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ ### Career summary **Electorate.** Hipkins won the Labour-held Rimutaka seat (renamed Remutaka in 2020) in 2008 after Paul Swain retired, beating union official Paul Chalmers for the nomination. His majorities: 753 (2008), 3,286 (2011), 6,664 (2014), 8,609 (2017), 8,859 (2023); in 2020 he polled 20,497 votes (official results via [electionresults.govt.nz 2011](http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2011/electorate-43.html), [2014](http://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-44.html), [2017](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-44.html), [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-42.html), [2023](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-42.html)). **Opposition, 2008–2017.** Spokesperson for internal affairs in his first term; under David Shearer he entered the shadow cabinet as education and state services spokesperson and became Labour's chief whip; he kept education under David Cunliffe, Andrew Little and Jacinda Ardern and was also shadow Leader of the House from 2014 ([Parliament profile](https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/members-of-parliament/hipkins-chris/)). **Minister, 2017–2023.** In the Sixth Labour Government he was Minister of Education and Leader of the House (26 Oct 2017 – 25 Jan 2023), Minister for the Public Service (2017–2023), Minister of Health (2 Jul – 6 Nov 2020, after David Clark resigned), Minister for COVID-19 Response (6 Nov 2020 – 14 Jun 2022) and Minister of Police (14 Jun 2022 – 25 Jan 2023), earning a reputation as the government's "fixer" ([The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/21-01-2023/the-guy-just-lives-for-diy-what-to-expect-from-prime-minister-chris-hipkins); [DPMC ministerial list Nov 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf)). **Prime Minister, 2023.** After Jacinda Ardern resigned, Hipkins was the only nominee for the Labour leadership (21–22 January 2023) and was sworn in as the 41st Prime Minister on 25 January 2023, with Carmel Sepuloni as the first Pasifika deputy prime minister ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/chris-hipkins-sworn-in-as-prime-minister-carmel-sepuloni-as-deputy-jacinda-ardern-vacates-top-job/IERZGZV2BFAE5AWLNJHMMGHYQ4/)). He led Labour to defeat at the October 2023 election (26.91% of the party vote, 34 seats) and conceded on election night ([Electoral Commission](https://elections.nz/media-and-news/2023/official-results-for-the-2023-general-election/); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/500185/election-2023-labour-s-chris-hipkins-concedes-congratulates-national-on-results)). He remained caretaker PM until Christopher Luxon was sworn in on 27 November 2023. **Opposition leader, 2023–present.** He took the ministerial services and national security & intelligence spokesperson roles in his shadow cabinet ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/503581/labour-party-leader-chris-hipkins-reveals-new-shadow-cabinet)) and in March 2025 reshuffled it and created an economic team led by Barbara Edmonds ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/544048/chris-hipkins-announces-new-labour-economic-team-tangi-utikere-promoted)). ## Record & notable actions - **Education (2017–2023):** legislated to stop new charter schools; all 12 existing charter schools became state-integrated or special-character schools by September 2018 ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2018/09/all-nz-charter-schools-now-approved-to-become-state-integrated.html)). Abolished National Standards and reviewed NCEA. Merged the 16 polytechnics and the industry training organisations into Te Pūkenga (from April 2020), a reform that by 2022 faced low enrolments, deficits and senior resignations ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/395722/government-confirms-major-overhaul-of-polytechnics-apprenticeships); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/waikato-times/300647698/minister-rules-out-te-pkenga-commissioner-at-this-time)). Declined Victoria University's proposed renaming to "University of Wellington" in 2018 ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/education/109441495/victoria-university-of-wellington-name-change-rejected-by-minister)). - **COVID-19 response (2020–2022):** introduced mask mandates on public transport, pre-departure testing, the My Vaccine Pass and the COVID-19 Response (Vaccinations) Legislation Act 2021 (vaccine-mandate framework) ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/456455/mandate-legislation-pushed-through-parliament-amid-fierce-opposition)); oversaw MIQ, including the January 2022 pause of the MIQ lottery ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/459786/government-postpones-next-miq-lottery-due-to-spike-of-omicron-cases-at-border)); announced in October 2022 the end of most COVID powers and a Royal Commission of Inquiry ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/476919/government-signals-covid-19-inquiry-in-the-works)). - **As Prime Minister (2023):** a "policy bonfire" scrapping or deferring the TVNZ–RNZ merger, the biofuel mandate, lowering the voting age to 16, the Clean Car Upgrade and much of the speed-reduction programme, and delaying social insurance and hate-speech law, with funds redirected to cost-of-living support ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/483875/watch-tvnz-rnz-merger-scrapped-income-insurance-and-hate-speech-laws-delayed); [1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/03/13/pms-policy-bonfire-voting-age-bill-transport-schemes-reprioritsed/)); led the response to the Auckland Anniversary floods and Cyclone Gabrielle; Budget 2023 removed $5 prescription fees, extended 20 hours ECE to two-year-olds and made public transport free for under-13s ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/490161/budget-2023-at-a-glance-what-you-need-to-know)); signed the NZ–EU free trade agreement on 9 July 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/493457/new-zealand-signs-free-trade-deal-with-european-union-after-years-of-negotiations)); ruled out a capital gains or wealth tax for the 2023 term ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/493596/hipkins-rules-out-capital-gains-tax-wealth-tax-if-labour-re-elected)). - **In opposition:** called for a Gaza ceasefire (November 2023) and in September 2025 said New Zealand should recognise the situation in Gaza as genocide ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/573334/nz-govt-will-not-respond-on-latest-accusation-of-genocide-in-gaza)); in April 2026 committed Labour's votes to pass the NZ–India free trade agreement, which NZ First opposed ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/593185/chris-hipkins-announces-labour-will-back-india-free-trade-deal)). - **Conscience votes:** voted for the Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill in 2013 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/gay-marriage-how-mps-voted/WLPKK4734FBZEKJIDHBFO4MWFA/)). - **Member's bills:** Electricity (Renewable Preference) Amendment Bill (defeated at first reading, 2010); Education (Charter Schools Abolition) Amendment Bill (defeated at first reading, 2016) ([Parliament](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/00DBHOH_BILL68842_1/education-charter-schools-abolition-amendment-bill)). ## Controversies - **Charlotte Bellis MIQ case (2022):** as COVID-19 Response Minister he publicly released details about pregnant journalist Charlotte Bellis's emergency MIQ application; she said she had not consented and disputed his account. In June 2022 he formally apologised for releasing personal information without consent and for inaccurate comments ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/covid-19-omicron-chris-hipkins-formally-apologises-over-charlotte-bellis-emergency-miq-saga/DX35AVZARU5RPUFTFUKDCNMK5A/)). - **Remarks about Bill English (2022):** apologised to former PM Bill English after suggesting in the House that English had favoured his brothers with government contracts ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/129959240/chris-hipkins-apologises-to-bill-english-for-dragging-family-into-debate)). - **As PM he dealt with several ministerial resignations/dismissals** — Stuart Nash, Meka Whaitiri, Michael Wood, Kiri Allan and Jan Tinetti's referral to the Privileges Committee (see those profiles). - 16th Deputy Leader of the New Zealand Labour Party (2013–2014) | | **Wikipedia** | [David Parker (New Zealand politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Parker_%28New_Zealand_politician%29) | ## Current status Parker announced on 8 April 2025 that he would leave Parliament, denying it was due to internal disputes over tax policy; his resignation took effect on 12 May 2025 and Vanushi Walters replaced him as list MP and shadow attorney-general ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/557515/labour-stalwart-and-former-cabinet-minister-david-parker-resigns-from-parliament); [NZ Gazette](https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2025-ps2424)). He is not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Born in 1960 in Roxburgh and raised in Dunedin (Otago Boys' High School), Parker graduated BCom and LLB from the University of Otago and co-founded the Dunedin Community Law Centre while a student ([Beehive biography](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/minister/biography/david-parker)). He practised resource-management and civil litigation law (managing partner of Anderson Lloyd), ran a café, and was a business manager for entrepreneur Howard Paterson, serving as founding chief executive of companies including A2 Corporation and Blis Technologies ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/electricity-sparks-parkers-political-ambitions/5P5W47CPHOA3OFS7ODDM6IN3KQ/)). He has three children with his former wife, poet Sue Wootton. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 47th | 2002–2005 | Otago | 47 | Labour | | 48th | 2005–2008 | List | 37 | Labour | | 49th | 2008–2011 | List | 17 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | List | 4 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | List | 2 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 10 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | List | 9 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–2025 | List | 13 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 32nd Attorney-General of New Zealand | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 16th Minister for the Environment | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 12th Minister for Trade and Export Growth | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 7th Minister for Economic Development | 26 October 2017 | 27 June 2019 | Jacinda Ardern | | Deputy Leader of the Opposition | 15 September 2013 | 30 September 2014 | | | 16th Deputy Leader of the New Zealand Labour Party | 15 September 2013 | 30 September 2014 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **Otago MP 2002–2005** (an upset win by 648 votes from list position 47); list MP 2005–2025 after losing Otago (2005), Waitaki (2008) and contesting Epsom (2011, 2017). - **Fifth Labour Government:** Attorney-General, Minister of Transport, Energy and Climate Change Issues from October 2005; resigned in March 2006 over a Companies Office filing allegation, was cleared, and returned to Cabinet in May 2006; later Minister of State Services and acting Environment Minister. - **Opposition 2008–2017:** finance spokesperson and economic policy architect for Labour's 2011 and 2014 platforms (capital gains tax, raising the pension age); deputy leader under David Cunliffe (2013–2014) and interim leader after the 2014 election; finished third in the 2014 leadership vote ([Stuff](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/63305825/Andrew-Little-new-Labour-Party-leader-by-a-whisker)). Later foreign affairs, trade, environment spokesperson and shadow attorney-general. - **Sixth Labour Government 2017–2023:** Attorney-General throughout; Minister for the Environment (2017–2023), Trade and Export Growth (2017–2020), Economic Development (2017–2019), Associate Finance; from 2020 also Oceans and Fisheries and Revenue; briefly Transport (2023). Dubbed "the minister of almost everything" ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/103235167/national-portrait-minister-of-almost-everything-david-parker)). - **Opposition 2023–2025:** shadow attorney-general and foreign affairs spokesperson; chair of the Regulations Review Committee. ## Record & notable actions - **Foreign-buyer ban:** led the Overseas Investment Amendment Act 2018 banning most foreign purchases of existing homes ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2018/aug/15/tenants-on-our-own-land-new-zealand-bans-sale-of-homes-to-foreign-buyers)). - **Trade:** signed the CPTPP (March 2018), led ratification of PACER Plus, launched UK FTA talks, and cancelled the Saudi "sheep deal" he had exposed in opposition ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/government-axes-saudi-sheep-deal/7KXXQSKRAU26OR2A737MPGM2TY/)). - **Resource management:** replaced the RMA with the Natural and Built Environment Act 2023 and Spatial Planning Act 2023 (passed 16 August 2023; repealed by the next government in December 2023) ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/government-passes-rma-replacement-bills-ending-30-years-of-rma/EUKOHYGWNNA3TDZYQYRI64446U/)); Essential Freshwater rules including winter-grazing controls (2020), criticised by farm lobbies as unworkable and by some scientists as too weak. - **Emissions Trading Scheme:** as climate change minister in 2008 he legislated the NZ ETS ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/climate-change-bill-becomes-law/BXWMGB3XSP4X6BJHJECTRAFI54/)). - **Attorney-General:** steered the COVID-19 Public Health Response Act 2020 (the High Court later found the first nine days of the 2020 lockdown, while justified, were not lawful) ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/423917/high-court-rules-some-of-covid-19-level-4-lockdown-was-unlawful)); oversaw the appointment of Helen Winkelmann as Chief Justice and of Joe Williams, the first Māori Supreme Court judge; passed the Bill of Rights (Declarations of Inconsistency) Amendment Act 2022. - **Tax fairness:** commissioned IRD research (2023) finding the wealthiest families paid a lower effective tax rate than most New Zealanders ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/488705/wealthiest-paying-tax-at-much-lower-rate-than-most-other-new-zealanders-ird-report)); passed the Tax Principles Reporting Act 2023, repealed under urgency in December 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/505298/parliament-repeals-tax-principles-reporting-law-under-urgency)). - **Conscience votes:** for civil unions (2004), marriage equality (2013), and the End of Life Choice Act (2019); against the 2003 euthanasia bill. ## Controversies - **2006 resignation:** resigned as Attorney-General and from Cabinet after a former business partner alleged he filed an incorrect Companies Office declaration; the Companies Office cleared him and he was reappointed ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/parker-heads-back-into-the-cabinet/G5FSJ3CZB4UEZG7X4VFSGOKBJA/)). - **Clare Curran hiring (2007):** the State Services Commission cleared him of improper pressure in suggesting the environment ministry hire Labour activist Clare Curran, though critics disputed the finding ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/no-ministerial-pressure-in-curran-job-report/LXTB3L3NSF3CFOBVXXP6DMOXKY/)). - **GST on KiwiSaver fees (2022):** a proposal to apply GST to KiwiSaver fees was dropped after a backlash; the 2022 cost-of-living payment was also criticised for paying people who were not eligible ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/473822/government-drops-plans-to-charge-gst-on-kiwisaver-fees)). - **Resignation as revenue minister (July 2023):** quit the portfolio, calling it "untenable" after Hipkins ruled out his wealth/capital gains tax work; some commentators called the timing petulant, others principled ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/132611615/david-parker-untenable-to-remain-revenue-minister-after-wealth-tax-rejection); [NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/claire-trevett-david-parkers-ill-timed-bout-of-principle-on-taxes-delivers-a-headache-for-chris-hipkins/2R5I3YCCKJEM3JLBMLI3STGFEU/)). - **EPA chair dismissal (2023):** removed Rob Campbell as Environmental Protection Authority chair after Campbell publicly criticised National's Three Waters stance in breach of neutrality expectations ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/485149/ousted-health-boss-rob-campbell-also-dumped-as-chair-of-epa)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - He graduated BA (Hons) in political studies from the University of Otago (1995), was Otago University Students' Association president (1993) and co-president of the national students' association (1996) ([NZ Listener](http://www.listener.co.nz/current-affairs/politics/interview-labour-deputy-grant-robertson/)). He was a diplomat with MFAT from 1997 to 2001 (including a UN posting and managing the Samoa aid programme), then an adviser to minister Marian Hobbs and to Prime Minister Helen Clark, and later worked for the University of Otago in Wellington. He lives in Wellington with his partner Alf Kaiwai (civil union 2009) and was New Zealand's first openly gay deputy prime minister ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/cabinets-grant-robertson-new-zealand-c840239beabda3fd6f3fbdd81fd5ea4f)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | Wellington Central | 46 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | Wellington Central | 14 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Wellington Central | 3 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Wellington Central | 4 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Wellington Central | 3 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–2024 | List | 4 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 10th Vice-Chancellor of the University of Otago | 1 July 2024 | present | | | 19th Deputy Prime Minister of New Zealand | 6 November 2020 | 25 January 2023 | Jacinda Ardern | | 29th Minister of Foreign Affairs | 11 November 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 12th Minister of Disarmament and Arms Control | 11 November 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 42nd Minister of Finance | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 12th Leader of the House | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 ; Acting: 25 January 2023 – 1 February 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 11th Minister for Sport and Recreation | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 4th Minister for Infrastructure | 6 November 2020 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 13th Minister for Racing | 6 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | 19th Minister Responsible for the Earthquake Commission | 27 June 2019 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | Deputy Leader of the Opposition | 13 December 2011 | 17 September 2013 | | | Deputy Leader of the Labour Party | 13 December 2011 | 17 September 2013 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **Wellington Central, 2008–2023.** Won the seat in 2008 (majority 1,904 over Stephen Franks), then held it with majorities of 6,376 (2011), 8,267 (2014), 9,963 (2017, over Nicola Willis) and 18,878 (2020, over Willis) ([2008](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2008/electorate-59.html), [2011](http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2011/electorate-59.html), [2014](https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-60.html), [2017](https://electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-60.html), [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-60.html)). In 2023 he stood list-only and returned as a list MP ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/483193/grant-robertson-goes-list-only-will-not-contest-wellington-central)). - **Opposition, 2008–2017.** Spokesperson for state services, tertiary education and (from 2011) health; deputy leader under David Shearer (13 Dec 2011 – 17 Sep 2013). Ran for leader in 2013 (won most caucus votes but lost to David Cunliffe on members' and affiliates' votes) and 2014 (lost to Andrew Little 50.52%–49.48% after preferences) ([Stuff 2013](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/9166765/Cunliffe-wins-Labour-leadership); [Stuff 2014](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/63305825/Andrew-Little-new-Labour-Party-leader-by-a-whisker)). Finance spokesperson from November 2014; chaired Labour's Future of Work Commission (report 2016). - **Minister of Finance, 26 Oct 2017 – 27 Nov 2023,** throughout the Ardern and Hipkins governments; also Minister for Sport and Recreation (2017–2023), Earthquake Commission (2019–2020), Infrastructure (2020–2023), Racing (2020–2022), Deputy Prime Minister (6 Nov 2020 – 25 Jan 2023, after Kelvin Davis declined the role), Leader of the House and Minister for Cyclone Recovery under Hipkins (2023), and briefly Minister of Foreign Affairs in the caretaker period (Nov 2023) ([DPMC ministerial list 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131290992/pm-chris-hipkins-announces-ministers-to-lead-regional-cyclone-recovery-efforts)). - **After January 2023:** declined to seek the leadership when Ardern resigned ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/01/19/grant-robertson-says-he-will-not-stand-as-next-labour-leader/)). Finance and racing spokesperson in opposition until he announced his retirement on 20 February 2024. ## Record & notable actions - Delivered six Budgets (2018–2023) as finance minister, including the pandemic-era budgets; he was the government's lead on the economic response to COVID-19 and often deputised for Ardern at pandemic briefings ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/opinion/123133786/election-2020-why-kelvin-davis-will-probably-be-the-next-deputy-prime-minister)). - Member's bill: Ethical Investment (Crown Financial Institutions) Bill (2010), defeated at first reading ([RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/stories/2010/08/05/d20e2514bc14)). - Retained the title "The Honourable" on retirement from the Executive Council (December 2023) ([NZ Gazette](https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2023-vr5732)). ## Controversies - In February 2021 he withdrew from a weekly slot on Magic Talk after host Peter Williams asked him about the World Economic Forum's "Great Reset", saying he did not want to keep shooting down conspiracy theories ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/entertainment/tv-radio/124301816/grant-robertson-axes-weekly-interview-on-magic-talk-radio-show)). - # Jacinda Ardern | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1980-07-26 — Hamilton, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | Mount Albert | | **Parliaments** | 49, 50, 51, 52, 53 | | **First elected** | 2008 | | **Key roles** | 40th Prime Minister of New Zealand (2017–2023)
17th Leader of the Labour Party (2017–2023)
36th Leader of the Opposition (2017)
17th Deputy Leader of the Labour Party (2017)
Member of the New Zealand Parliament (2008–2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Jacinda Ardern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacinda_Ardern) | ## Current status Dame Jacinda Ardern left Parliament at the 2023 election and is not involved in the 2026 campaign as a candidate. After office she took up dual fellowships at the Harvard Kennedy School (2023) ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/new-zealand-jacinda-ardern-harvard-university-d9d82f742e79815e91687bd54213bd53)), became a trustee of Prince William's Earthshot Prize ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/uk-65180096)), was appointed Special Envoy for the Christchurch Call by Chris Hipkins in April 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/487340/former-pm-jacinda-ardern-appointed-as-christchurch-call-envoy)), and published her memoir *A Different Kind of Power* in June 2025, which won the 2026 E. H. McCormick Prize for best first book of general non-fiction ([NZ Book Awards](https://www.nzbookawards.nz/new-zealand-book-awards/2026-awards/winners/)). In February 2026 *The Guardian* reported that she and her family had moved to Sydney ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/feb/26/jacinda-ardern-living-in-australia-former-nz-new-zealand-pm)). She was made a Dame Grand Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in 2023 ([DPMC](https://www.dpmc.govt.nz/publications/kings-birthday-and-coronation-honours-list-2023)). ## Biography Born 26 July 1980 in Hamilton and raised in Morrinsville and Murupara (her father was a police officer), Ardern joined Labour at 17 and graduated from the University of Waikato with a Bachelor of Communication Studies in 2001 ([Waikato University profile](https://apps.mngt.waikato.ac.nz/Newsroom/StudentProfile/3724)). She worked as a researcher for Phil Goff and Helen Clark, then in London as a policy adviser in the UK Cabinet Office, and in 2008 was elected president of the International Union of Socialist Youth. She was raised in the LDS Church but left it in 2005, citing her support for gay rights ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/lifestyle/news/article.cfm?c_id=6&objectid=11789352)). She married broadcaster Clarke Gayford in January 2024; their daughter Neve was born on 21 June 2018 while Ardern was prime minister ([BBC](https://www.bbc.com/news/world-asia-44568537)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | List | 20 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | List | 13 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | List | 5 | Labour | | 51st | 2017 (by-election)– | Mount Albert | | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Mount Albert | 1 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Mount Albert | 1 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 40th Prime Minister of New Zealand | 26 October 2017 | 25 January 2023 | | | 17th Leader of the Labour Party | 1 August 2017 | 22 January 2023 | | | 36th Leader of the Opposition | 1 August 2017 | 26 October 2017 | | | 17th Deputy Leader of the Labour Party | 7 March 2017 | 1 August 2017 | | | Member of the New Zealand Parliament | 8 November 2008 | 15 April 2023 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **List MP, 2008–2017.** Entered Parliament from list position 20 in 2008 (losing the Waikato electorate). Stood in Auckland Central in 2011 and 2014, losing to National's Nikki Kaye by 717 and then 600 votes ([2011 results](http://www.electionresults.org.nz/electionresults_2011/electorate-1.html), [2014 results](http://www.electionresults.org.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-1.html)). Spokesperson for youth affairs (under Goff), social development (No. 4 in Shearer's shadow cabinet, 2011), then justice, children, small business and arts (under Little, 2014). - **Mount Albert, 2017–2023.** Won the February 2017 Mount Albert by-election with about 77% of the vote ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11807614)); majorities of 15,264 (2017) and 21,246 (2020) ([2017](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-27.html), [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-24.html)). - **Deputy leader (7 Mar 2017) and leader (1 Aug 2017).** Became leader seven weeks before the 2017 election after Andrew Little resigned; Labour rose from 24% to the low 40s in polls ("Jacindamania") and won 46 seats ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=11922098)). - **Prime Minister, 26 Oct 2017 – 25 Jan 2023.** Led a Labour–NZ First coalition with Green confidence and supply (2017–2020), then the first single-party majority government under MMP after winning 65 seats and 50% of the party vote in 2020 ([Electoral Commission](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/)). Also Minister for National Security and Intelligence, Arts, Culture and Heritage, and the first Minister for Child Poverty Reduction. - **Resignation.** Announced on 19 January 2023 that she no longer had "enough in the tank", resigned as leader on 22 January and as PM on 25 January, and left Parliament in April 2023 ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2023/jan/19/jacinda-ardern-resigns-as-prime-minister-of-new-zealand)). ## Record & notable actions - **Christchurch mosque attacks (2019):** led the national response to the 15 March 2019 attacks in which 51 people were killed; within a month Parliament banned most semi-automatic weapons and high-capacity magazines, followed by a buy-back ([NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2019/04/10/world/asia/new-zealand-guns-jacinda-ardern.html)); co-founded the Christchurch Call with Emmanuel Macron ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12226274)). - **COVID-19:** border closure (March 2020), alert-level 4 lockdown, elimination strategy until October 2021, vaccine rollout from February 2021 ([NYT](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/10/04/world/australia/new-zealand-covid-zero.html)). The MIQ system left many citizens unable to return; in April 2022 the High Court found aspects of MIQ unjustifiably limited citizens' right to enter New Zealand ([High Court judgment](https://www.courtsofnz.govt.nz/assets/Uploads/Judgments-online/2022-NZHC-832.pdf)). - **Child poverty and welfare:** Child Poverty Reduction Act targets; the 2018 Families Package (26 weeks' paid parental leave, Best Start payment) ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/feature/supporting-new-zealand-families-0)); free school lunches (Ka Ora, Ka Ako); benefit increases; first year of tertiary study fees-free (2018). - **Climate:** Zero Carbon Act passed with cross-party support (2019); declared a climate emergency in December 2020 ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2020/dec/02/new-zealand-declares-a-climate-change-emergency)). - **Tax:** ruled out a capital gains tax under her leadership in April 2019 after the Tax Working Group recommended one ([RNZ](https://www.radionz.co.nz/news/on-the-inside/387347/week-in-politics-labour-s-biggest-campaign-burden-scrapped)); bright-line test extended to 10 years (2021). - **Other:** formal apology for the Dawn Raids (2021); cannabis referendum (2020, narrowly defeated; she disclosed afterwards she voted yes) ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/123261775/pm-defends-no-comment-stance-on-cannabis-referendum)). - **Conscience votes:** voted for marriage equality (2013) and for the Abortion Legislation Act 2020 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/412087/abortion-legislation-bill-passes-third-and-final-reading-in-parliament)). ## Controversies - **Clare Curran (2018):** criticised for initially only removing Curran from Cabinet over an undisclosed meeting rather than dismissing her; Curran later resigned ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2018/09/prime-minister-jacinda-ardern-accepts-clare-curran-s-resignation-as-a-minister.html)). - **Labour staffer sexual-assault complaint (2019):** her account that she had been told the complaint did not involve sexual assault was questioned by media; party president Nigel Haworth resigned ([The Spinoff timeline](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/11-09-2019/timeline-labour-staffer-misconduct-inquiry/)). - **Hot-mic remark (2022):** called ACT leader David Seymour an "arrogant prick" in the House; she apologised and the pair later auctioned a framed copy for charity ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/130764372/jacinda-ardern-apologises-for-calling-david-seymour-an-arrogant-prick)). - **Undelivered targets:** critics, including former coalition partner Winston Peters, said her government under-delivered on housing (e.g. KiwiBuild), child poverty and inequality; her approval fell to 29% by late 2022 ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2022/dec/24/jacinda-arderns-popularity-plummeted-this-year-things-could-get-worse-in-2023); [Reuters](https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/new-zealands-ardern-leaves-legacy-kindness-disappointments-2023-01-19/)). - **Threats and abuse:** she was the target of sustained abuse and threats from anti-mandate protesters; a man was convicted of threatening to kill her ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/nz-news/350300416/richard-sivell-run-almost-two-years-appears-court)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources -
