16th Minister for Women (2020–2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Jan Tinetti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Tinetti) | ## Current status Tinetti is No. 10 in Labour's shadow cabinet, with workplace relations and safety, social investment, early childhood education and child poverty reduction since March 2025, and is again Labour's candidate in Tauranga (list No. 15) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)). ## Biography Born in Hokitika in 1968, Tinetti grew up inside Templeton Hospital and Training School near Christchurch, where her father was secretary — an experience of an institution for people with intellectual disabilities she cited in her maiden statement ([Hansard](https://www.parliament.nz/mi/pb/hansard-debates/rhr/document/HansS_20171116_056700000/tinetti-jan)). She trained at Christchurch College of Education (1990), taught in Southland, Greymouth and Tauranga, and was a primary principal for 20 years, latterly at Merivale School, Tauranga; she served on the NZEI national executive and holds a Master of Education (Canterbury, 2016). She is married to David Merton and has two children; she was treated for breast cancer in 2019 ([Newsroom](https://www.newsroom.co.nz/new-minister-driven-by-injustices-witnessed-as-a-child)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 15 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | List | 32 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | List | 6 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 48th Minister of Education | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 36th Minister of Internal Affairs | 6 November 2020 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 16th Minister for Women | 6 November 2020 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 10 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Spokesperson for Workplace Relations and Safety - Spokesperson for Social Investment - Spokesperson for Early Childhood Education - Spokesperson for Child Poverty Reduction _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ ### Career summary - **Tauranga candidate** in 2017, 2020, the 2022 by-election and 2023, losing to Simon Bridges (by 11,252 in 2017 and 1,856 in 2020) and then Sam Uffindell (by-election 2022; by 9,370 in 2023); a list MP since 2017 ([2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-52.html); [2023](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-52.html); [RNZ by-election](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/469380/national-s-uffindell-easily-wins-tauranga-by-election)). - **Minister, 2020–2023:** Minister of Internal Affairs, Minister for Women and Associate Minister of Education (Nov 2020); Minister of Education and Child Poverty Reduction (No. 6 in Cabinet) from 31 January 2023 ([Beehive list](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2023-01/Ministerial%20List%20as%20announced%20on%2031%20January%202023.pdf)). - **Opposition:** education and women (2023–2025); workplace relations, social investment, ECE and child poverty (from March 2025). ## Controversies - **Privileges Committee referral (2023):** Speaker Adrian Rurawhe referred her to the Privileges Committee after she delayed correcting a February 2023 statement to the House that she had no role in the timing of school attendance data release; she was told of the error but did not correct it until 2 May. On 29 June 2023 the committee found she had not intentionally misled the House but had acted with a "high degree of negligence", and required her to apologise to the House. Hipkins kept her as minister ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/490981/education-minister-jan-tinetti-s-delay-in-correcting-record-to-be-investigated); [RNZ report](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/492852/jan-tinetti-made-error-of-judgement-that-misled-parliament-privileges-committee-finds)). During the hearing National's Michael Woodhouse apologised for calling her a "good girl" ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/491860/senior-national-mp-michael-woodhouse-apologises-for-calling-education-minister-jan-tinetti-a-good-girl)). - After losing Tauranga in 2023 she said a "weight had been lifted", a remark criticised by breakfast-TV hosts ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/10/election-2023-am-hosts-slam-bizarre-reactions-from-ousted-labour-mps-jan-tinetti-dan-rosewarne.html)). ## 2026 candidacy - won Rangitata in 2020 by 4,408 over Megan Hands — a surprise gain in a seat National had held since 2005; lost it to National's James Meager by 10,846 in 2023 and returned on the list ([2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-40.html); He is married to Moira; they have three children. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | List | 33 | Labour | | 50th | 2014– | List | 23 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Te Tai Tokerau | 18 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Te Tai Tokerau | 2 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Te Tai Tokerau | 2 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–2024 | List | 2 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 18th Deputy Leader of the Labour Party | 1 August 2017 | 7 November 2023 | | | 14th Minister of Corrections | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 1st Minister for Māori–Crown Relations | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 3rd Minister for Children | 6 November 2020 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 36th Minister of Tourism | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | Deputy Leader of the Opposition | 1 August 2017 | 26 October 2017 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **List MP 2008–2011;** lost Te Tai Tokerau to Hone Harawira in 2008, the 2011 by-election and the 2011 general election, and left Parliament. - **Returned May 2014** as a list MP when Shane Jones resigned, then won Te Tai Tokerau from Harawira in September 2014 — ending Internet-Mana's parliamentary presence — after endorsements from John Key and Winston Peters ([Stuff](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/10524510/Davis-win-a-critical-blow-for-Harawira-Internet-Mana)). Acting prime minister on several occasions. ## Record & notable actions - **Prison population:** as Corrections Minister he set out to reduce Māori imprisonment; the imprisonment rate fell from about 213 to 149 per 100,000 during his tenure, helped by bail support and earlier parole-readiness programmes — National's Mark Mitchell argued the focus should have been on reducing crime ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/election-2023-labour-dumps-prison-population-reduction-target/AAL2EXLUGBFNHJ27VJSRS2EPHY/); [The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/02-11-2018/kelvin-davis-has-a-cunning-plan-to-cut-the-prison-population-and-its-working)). - **Te Arawhiti:** established the Office for Māori Crown Relations in 2018 ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/te-arawhiti-%E2%80%98bridge%E2%80%99-better-m%C4%81ori-crown-relations-launched-parliament)). - **Oranga Tamariki:** declined to back chief executive Grainne Moss (who resigned in January 2021), set up a ministerial advisory board, and began devolving services to iwi and community providers ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/435242/new-four-person-board-to-oversee-oranga-tamariki-overhaul)). - **In opposition (2014–2017):** exposed problems at Serco-run Mount Eden prison, after which Serco lost the contract ([Stuff](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/70619419/labours-kelvin-davis-says-mt-eden-prison-guard-revelations-are-corruption)); his KiwiBuild member's bill (10,000 homes a year) was defeated in 2017. - **Conscience votes:** voted for the End of Life Choice Act 2019 and the Abortion Legislation Act 2020. Broke with Labour policy to support the two charter schools in his electorate, which became state-integrated ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/335647/davis-threatens-to-resign-if-two-charter-schools-closed-down)). ## Controversies - **Parliamentary performance:** his performances as acting PM in the House were widely criticised (one Stuff columnist called a 2017 appearance a "trainwreck") ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/opinion/98982731/labour-has-a-problem--we-need-to-talk-about-acting-prime-minister-kelvin-davis)). - **Waikeria Prison riot (2020–21):** criticised by National and Te Pāti Māori for staying silent during the six-day standoff; he pushed back on parts of the Chief Ombudsman's later report on Corrections ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/kelvin-davis-pushes-back-on-the-ombudsmans-damming-corrections-report/CYJFPMX3IFBJNEHR3STID6VNV4/)). - **"Vanilla lens" remark (2022):** told ACT's Karen Chhour (who is Ngāpuhi) to stop looking through a "vanilla lens"; ACT called it racist and he apologised to her by phone ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/475720/minister-davis-apologises-over-comments-to-act-s-karen-chhour)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - His member's bill allowing on-licence premises open on Good Friday, Anzac Day morning and Christmas Day to sell alcohol under normal conditions passed its third reading 66–55 on a conscience vote on 1 April 2026 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/591281/bill-to-ease-holiday-alcohol-restrictions-passes-final-reading-in-parliament)). ## Biography Born in Eketāhuna in 1985 and adopted into a long-established Wairarapa Labour family, McAnulty was head boy of Chanel College (2002) and gained a BA, PGDipArts and an MA in politics from the University of Otago ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/kieran-mcanulty-why-the-wairarapa-mp-is-rural-to-the-core/SVEH6NYJJZHJNFPGBO4CSZF7PU/)). His battered red Mazda ute became a campaign trademark until he sold it for charity in 2021 ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2021/09/19/labours-mcanulty-swapping-famous-red-ute-for-hybrid-wagon/)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 38 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Wairarapa | 26 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | List | 16 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 20th Minister of Local Government | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 2nd Minister for Rural Communities | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 28th Minister for Emergency Management | 14 June 2022 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 14th Minister for Racing | 14 June 2022 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | Chief Government Whip in the House of Representatives | 2 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 7 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - **Wairarapa:** lost to National's Alastair Scott in 2014 and 2017 (entering Parliament from list position 38 in 2017); won the seat in 2020 by 6,545 votes over Mike Butterick; lost it to Butterick in 2023 and returned on the list ([2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-58.html); [2023](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-58.html)). - **Opposition:** No. 7 in the shadow cabinet, with housing, local government and regional development (2023); Shadow Leader of the House; from March 2025 housing, infrastructure and public investment. ## Record & notable actions - **Cyclone Gabrielle:** declared a national state of emergency on 14 February 2023 — only the third in New Zealand's history ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/state-national-emergency-declared)). - # Kiri Allan | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1984 — Te Karaka, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | East Coast | | **Parliaments** | 52, 53 | | **First elected** | 2017 | | **Key roles** | 51st Minister of Justice (2022–2023)
Minister for Regional Development (2023)
14th Minister of Conservation (2020–2022)
27th Minister for Emergency Management (2020–2022) | | **Wikipedia** | [Kiri Allan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kiri_Allan) | ## Current status Allan did not stand in 2023 and left Parliament at that election. After leaving she announced a book deal with Penguin and set up a lobbying consultancy — registered while she was still an MP, which drew "revolving door" criticism given she had been responsible for lobbying reform as justice minister ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/political-roundup-kiri-allan-latest-ex-labour-minister-to-move-into-lobbying/HBUTCMXLNRGQTGWLA2EFOGMGZY/)). She is not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Kiritapu Allan was born in 1984 in Te Karaka (Ngāti Ranginui, Ngāti Tūwharetoa) and raised whāngai by an aunt and uncle in Paengaroa and later Auckland, where she attended Auckland Girls' Grammar's reo Māori unit ([E-Tangata](https://e-tangata.co.nz/korero/kiri-allan-always-raising-eyebrows/)). She left school at 16, worked at KFC and as a fruit picker, then studied law and politics at Victoria University of Wellington, interning for Helen Clark and lawyer Annette Sykes. She worked at ChenPalmer and Kāhui Legal in Whakatāne. She has written about undergoing conversion therapy as a teenager ([The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/politics/19-02-2022/kiri-allan-my-conversion-therapy-story)). She was treated for stage 3 cervical cancer in 2021 and declared cancer-free that December ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/457582/mp-kiri-allan-given-all-clear-after-months-of-cervical-cancer-treatment)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 21 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | East Coast | 25 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 51st Minister of Justice | 14 June 2022 | 24 July 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | Minister for Regional Development | 1 February 2023 | 24 July 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 14th Minister of Conservation | 6 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | 27th Minister for Emergency Management | 6 November 2020 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **List MP 2017–2020** after losing East Coast to Anne Tolley; junior whip, chair of Labour's rural caucus. - **East Coast MP 2020–2023:** won the open seat by 6,331 votes over National's Tania Tapsell ([2020 results](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-09.html)). - **Minister:** Conservation and Emergency Management (Nov 2020 – Jun 2022) plus associate Arts, Culture and Heritage and Environment; Justice and Associate Finance from June 2022; under Hipkins (No. 10 in Cabinet) also Regional Development and Associate Transport, and a lead minister for the Cyclone Gabrielle response in Tairāwhiti ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/483394/prime-minister-chris-hipkins-reveals-cabinet-reshuffle)). Co-nominated Hipkins for the leadership in January 2023. ## Record & notable actions - Fronted the March 2021 Kermadec earthquake tsunami evacuations on the day her cancer diagnosis was confirmed ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300269974/kiri-allan-bit-of-a-superwoman-to-handle-tsunami-and-earthquake-response-on-same-day-as-medical-test-confirming-her-cancer-diagnosis)). - Passed the law creating the Matariki public holiday (first observed 2022) ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/464833/matariki-public-holiday-passes-into-law)). - As Justice Minister: repealed the three-strikes sentencing law (2022) ([Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/three-strikes-legislation-repeal-bill-passes-third-reading)); electoral law reforms (donations disclosure, Māori electoral option); expanded legal aid; announced a new ram-raid offence in July 2023. - **Conscience votes:** voted for the third readings of the End of Life Choice Bill and Abortion Legislation Bill (having voted against the euthanasia bill at second reading). ## Controversies - **RNZ speech (March 2023):** at the farewell of her then-fiancée Māni Dunlop from RNZ, she commented on RNZ's treatment of Māori staff; she accepted this could be seen as a minister directing a Crown entity and apologised ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/489511/rnz-releases-comments-from-kiri-allan-speech)). - **Meng Foon donations (April 2023):** she had properly declared 2020 campaign support from Race Relations Commissioner Meng Foon, but was criticised for not flagging a conflict of interest when she became the minister responsible for him ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/04/21/allan-declares-perceived-conflict-of-interest-after-foon-donation/)). - **Staff treatment (June–July 2023):** the heads of DOC and NEMA raised concerns about how staff in her office were treated; she apologised and received coaching ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/493729/east-coast-mp-kiri-allan-to-resume-duties-after-speaking-with-pm-on-staff-allegations)). - **Arrest and resignation (July 2023):** on 23 July 2023 she crashed her ministerial car into a parked car in Wellington, was arrested for careless driving and refusing to accompany a police officer, and received an excess-breath-alcohol infringement notice; she resigned all portfolios the next day and announced she would not stand again ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/494338/kiri-allan-charged-with-reckless-driving-and-resisting-arrest-resigns-as-justice-minister-pm-says); [1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/07/25/kiri-allan-announces-she-wont-stand-for-re-election/)). In May 2024 she pleaded guilty to both charges; she was fined $300 and ordered to pay $5,296 reparation for careless driving and discharged on the second charge ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/05/22/kiri-allan-pleads-guilty-on-day-trial-was-set-to-begin/)). She has spoken publicly about her mental health at the time and later disclosed ADHD and PTSD diagnoses ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/01/26/kiri-allan-opens-up-about-days-that-led-to-her-political-downfall/)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - parties/labour/people/louisa-wall/README: # Louisa Wall | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Labour | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1972-02-17 — Taupō, New Zealand | | **Electorate(s) held** | Manurewa | | **Parliaments** | 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, 53 | | **First elected** | 2008 | | **Wikipedia** | [Louisa Wall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Louisa_Wall) | ## Current status Wall left Parliament on 1 May 2022, saying her departure was part of an agreement made during the disputed 2020 Manurewa selection and that it was "not entirely my choice" ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/465300/departing-labour-mp-louisa-wall-this-was-not-entirely-my-choice)). She was then Ambassador for Gender Equality (Pacific), a newly created role that critics said was designed for her; it was disestablished after two years ([Newsroom](http://newsroom.co.nz/2022/05/31/inside-louisa-walls-diplomatic-sinecure/); [The Post](https://www.thepost.co.nz/politics/350212701/louisa-walls-ambassador-role-scrapped)). In 2023 RNZ reported she was considering standing for Te Pāti Māori, which did not happen ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/488115/former-labour-mp-louisa-wall-could-stand-for-te-pati-maori-in-manurewa)). ## Biography Born 17 February 1972 in Taupō (Ngāti Tūwharetoa, Ngāti Hineuru, Waikato), Wall is a double international: a Silver Fern (netball, 1989–1992) and a Black Fern (rugby, 1995–2001) who won the 1998 Women's Rugby World Cup ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11893700)). She holds social work and social policy degrees from Massey and worked in health research for the Health Research Council, the Children's Commissioner and Counties Manukau DHB. She married lawyer Prue Kapua in 2015. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 48th | 2008– | List | 46 | Labour | | 49th | 2011– | List | 43 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | Manurewa | none | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Manurewa | 12 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Manurewa | 26 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2022 | List | 27 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Career summary - List MP Feb–Nov 2008 and Apr–Nov 2011; **Manurewa MP 2011–2020** (majority 8,610 in 2011) — the first Māori Labour candidate to win a general electorate; list MP 2020–2022 after withdrawing from a disputed Manurewa selection won by Arena Williams ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=12335909)). - Chaired the Health Committee (2017–2020); never a minister. Stuff's Henry Cooke judged she achieved more than any other Labour MP in opposition (2008–2017) ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300553289/louisa-wall-achieved-a-lot-in-politics-but-sometimes-forgot-it-was-a-team-sport)). ## Record & notable actions - **Marriage equality:** her Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill passed 77–44 on 17 April 2013, making New Zealand the 13th country to legalise same-sex marriage ([TVNZ](http://tvnz.co.nz/national-news/mps-vote-legalise-same-sex-marriage-5409720)). - **Abortion safe areas:** her bill restoring safe zones around abortion services passed 108–12 on 16 March 2022 ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/128080358/safe-areas-abortion-law-passes-with-large-majority-in-parliament)). - **Revenge porn:** her Harmful Digital Communications amendment passed unanimously on 2 March 2022. - Supported the End of Life Choice Act at every stage; an outspoken critic of China's treatment of Uyghurs (Ardern said she spoke as IPAC co-chair, not for the government) ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2021/07/jacinda-ardern-distances-herself-from-labour-mp-louisa-wall-who-accused-china-of-harvesting-organs.html)). ## Controversies - **2020 Manurewa selection and exit:** she called her de-selection unconstitutional and alleged Ardern did not want her in caucus because she had backed David Cunliffe; Ardern did not attend her valedictory speech ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300563234/pm-jacinda-ardern-will-not-attend-louisa-walls-valedictory-speech)). - **Al Nisbet cartoons:** her complaint over 2013 cartoons about Māori and Pacific families was dismissed by the Human Rights Review Tribunal and on appeal, though the High Court called the cartoons objectively offensive ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/labour-mps-racist-cartoon-appeal-against-fairfax-media-dismissed/K4QZ7ZJHBFEK5G3COO2DOTA4E4/)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - On 3 August 2025 she announced she would not seek re-selection in Wigram and would stand on the list only ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/08/03/senior-labour-mp-wont-contest-electorate-will-stand-on-list-in-2026/)). Since March 2025 her portfolios have been energy and resources, manufacturing and industry, and associate finance (she gave up climate change) ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/544048/chris-hipkins-announces-new-labour-economic-team-tangi-utikere-promoted)). ## Biography Born 4 November 1973 and raised in Wigram, Christchurch, Woods attended Cathedral College and earned an MA and a PhD in history from the University of Canterbury; her doctorate examined Māori urbanisation and integration policy, 1942–1969 ([UC Research Repository](https://ir.canterbury.ac.nz/handle/10092/4352)). She was a business manager at Crop & Food Research and Plant & Food Research (2005–2008) ([The Press](http://www.stuff.co.nz/the-press/news/christchurch/4144405/Anderton-follower-chosen-for-Wigram)). Politically she began in the Alliance (1999–2002) and Jim Anderton's Progressive Party — she stood for the Progressives in Christchurch Central in 2005 — and joined Labour in 2007, the year she came second for the Christchurch mayoralty against Bob Parker. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 50th | 2011–2014 | Wigram | 47 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Wigram | 20 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Wigram | 6 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Wigram | 5 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | Wigram | 5 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 17th Minister of Energy and Resources | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 28th Minister of Housing | 27 June 2019 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 9th Minister for Building and Construction | 14 June 2022 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 5th Minister for Infrastructure | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | Minister for Economic Development (Acting) | 28 March 2023 | 12 April 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | Minister of Forestry (Acting) | 28 March 2023 | 12 April 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | Minister of Police (Acting) | 15 March 2023 | 20 March 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 26th Minister for Research, Science and Innovation | 26 October 2017 | 14 June 2022 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister for Greater Christchurch Regeneration | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | Minister for Government Digital Services | 26 August 2018 | 28 June 2019 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 4 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Spokesperson for Manufacturing and Industry - Spokesperson for Energy and Resources - Associate Spokesperson for Finance _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ ### Career summary - **Wigram, 2011–present.** Succeeded Jim Anderton; majorities of 1,500 (2011), 4,594 (2017), 14,770 (2020) and 1,179 (2023) ([2011](http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2011/electorate-63.html), [2017](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2017/electorate-details-64.html), [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-65.html), [2023](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-65.html)). - **Opposition, 2011–2017:** tertiary education spokesperson, then environment and climate change. - **Minister, 2017–2023:** Minister of Energy and Resources, Research, Science and Innovation, and Greater Christchurch Regeneration from 2017; Minister of Housing from 27 June 2019 (taking over from Phil Twyford); joint head of managed isolation and quarantine from June 2020; Associate Minister of Finance from 2020; held eleven ministerial portfolios in all, earning a reputation as Labour's "Ms Fix-it" ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/megan-woods-the-labour-partys-ms-fix-it-the-woman-called-in-to-clean-up-kiwibuild/EBZIOR3IQNG7ECFL3GUE5GPEEU/); [Parliament profile](https://www.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/members-of-parliament/woods-megan/)). - Chaired Labour's 2020 and 2023 election campaigns ([The Post](https://www.thepost.co.nz/a/politics/350015012/professionals-true-believers-and-mad-men-the-teams-behind-the-election-campaigns)). Considered a possible successor to Ardern in January 2023 but did not stand. ## Record & notable actions - **Oil and gas exploration ban (April 2018):** announced an end to new offshore oil and gas exploration permits, with existing permits continuing ([RNZ](https://www.radionz.co.nz/news/national/354816/oil-gas-exploration-move-a-kick-in-the-guts-for-taranaki-mayor)). - **Housing:** took over KiwiBuild after Twyford; in October 2021 announced, jointly with National leader Judith Collins and Environment Minister David Parker, the cross-party Medium Density Residential Standards (Resource Management (Enabling Housing Supply) Amendment Act) allowing up to three homes of up to three storeys on most urban sites ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/labour-and-national-join-forces-for-housing-crisis-fix-ending-decades-of-standoff/Z27M7UF7QFO4RMLNR7UQBQERZI/)). Opened Kāinga Ora's Te Mātāwai mixed-tenure development in 2023 ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/495077/te-matawai-prime-minister-chris-hipkins-opens-government-s-largest-public-housing-development)). In 2024 she criticised National's decision to let councils opt out of the bipartisan density rules ([OneRoof](https://www.oneroof.co.nz/news/ex-housing-minister-rare-moment-of-political-agreement-torpedoed-by-christopher-luxon-45717)). - **MIQ (2020–2022):** shared responsibility for managed isolation and quarantine ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/419375/housing-minister-megan-woods-to-oversee-managed-isolation-and-quarantine-facilities)). ## Controversies - **Progressive Home Ownership scheme (2021):** National's Nicola Willis called it a failure after it had cost $17 million and housed 12 families in seven months; Woods defended it ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/437079/progressive-home-ownership-scheme-houses-just-12-families-in-seven-months)). - parties/labour/people/meka-whaitiri/READ: # Meka Whaitiri > **This person's current profile is under [te-pati-maori](../../../te-pati-maori/people/meka-whaitiri/README.md).** They sat as a labour MP; this page is kept for their labour-era history and is not counted separately. | | | |---|---| | **Party** | Te Pāti Māori (formerly Labour) | | **Status (Oct 2026)** | Former MP | | **Born** | 1965-01-11 | | **Electorate(s) held** | Ikaroa-Rāwhiti | | **Parliaments** | 50, 51, 52, 53 | | **First elected** | 2013 | | **Key roles** | 63rd Minister of Customs (2020–2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Meka Whaitiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meka_Whaitiri) | ## Current status Whaitiri left Parliament after the 2023 election, which she contested as Te Pāti Māori's Ikaroa-Rāwhiti candidate, losing to Labour's Cushla Tangaere-Manuel by 2,843 votes ([2023 results](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-67.html)). She does not appear among 2026 candidates on policy.nz; Te Pāti Māori's 2026 Ikaroa-Rāwhiti candidate is Haley Maxwell ([policy.nz Ikaroa-Rāwhiti](https://policy.nz/2026/ikaroa-rawhiti-electorate/candidates/cushla-tangaere-manuel)). No reliable source was found for her activities since 2023. ## Biography Born 11 January 1965 in Manutuke near Gisborne (Rongowhakaata, Ngāti Kahungunu) and raised in Whakatu, Hastings; her mother was the model for Napier's Pania of the Reef statue. She was head girl of Karamu High School, worked in a freezing works, earned a master's in education from Victoria University of Wellington and played softball and netball at national level (a Silver Ferns non-travelling reserve) ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=10886303)). She worked for Parekura Horomia at the Department of Labour and in his ministerial office, for the Māori Women's Welfare League, and was chief executive of Ngāti Kahungunu Iwi Inc. (2009–2013). She has two sons. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 50th | 2013–2014 | Ikaroa-Rāwhiti | | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Ikaroa-Rāwhiti | 19 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Ikaroa-Rāwhiti | none | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Ikaroa-Rāwhiti | 28 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 63rd Minister of Customs | 6 November 2020 | 3 May 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **Ikaroa-Rāwhiti MP 2013–2023:** won the June 2013 by-election after Horomia's death (majority 1,659 over Mana's Te Hamua Nikora); majorities 4,673 (2014), 4,210 (2017) and 6,045 (2020) ([RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/214123/majority-drops-slightly-in-final-by-election-result); [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-67.html)). - **Minister:** Minister of Customs (outside Cabinet) 2017–2018 until stood down; reappointed Customs and Veterans, associate agriculture (animal welfare) and statistics (2020), Food Safety (2022), and lead Hawke's Bay cyclone recovery minister (March 2023). Co-chair of Labour's Māori caucus. - **Defection (3 May 2023):** announced she was leaving Labour to stand for Te Pāti Māori; Hipkins removed her portfolios. She is not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Born 21 August 1970 in Auckland, Mahuta is the daughter of Sir Robert Mahuta (adopted son of Māori King Korokī) and a first cousin of the late Kiingi Tūheitia ([E-Tangata](https://e-tangata.co.nz/korero/no-silver-spoon/)). She was educated at Rakaumanga kura in Huntly and Waikato Diocesan School, and holds an MA (Hons) in social anthropology from the University of Auckland. She is married to Gannin Ormsby. In 2016 she became the first woman MP to wear a moko kauae ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2016/aug/11/first-woman-mp-maori-facial-tattoo-nz-parliament-moko-kauae)); she was named one of the BBC's 100 Women in 2018. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 45th | 1996–1999 | List | 8 | Labour | | 46th | 1999–2002 | Te Tai Hauāuru | 10 | Labour | | 47th | 2002–2005 | Tainui | 19 | Labour | | 48th | 2005–2008 | Tainui | none | Labour | | 49th | 2008–2011 | Hauraki-Waikato | 10 | Labour | | 50th | 2011–2014 | Hauraki-Waikato | 12 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Hauraki-Waikato | 6 | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Hauraki-Waikato | none | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Hauraki-Waikato | 10 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 28th Minister of Foreign Affairs | 6 November 2020 | 11 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 11th Minister of Disarmament and Arms Control | 1 February 2023 | 11 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 12th Minister of Local Government | 26 October 2017 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 44th Minister for Māori Development | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **MP 1996–2023:** elected on the list in 1996 aged 26 (then the youngest MP); MP for Te Tai Hauāuru (1999–2002), Tainui (2002–2008) and Hauraki-Waikato (2008–2023). Became Mother of the House in October 2022 ([Parliament](https://www.parliament.nz/en/visit-and-learn/mps-and-parliaments-1854-onwards/members-of-parliament-longest-shortest-oldest-youngest/)). - **Fifth Labour Government:** Minister of Customs and Youth Affairs (2005), Local Government (2007–2008). - **Opposition 2008–2017:** spokesperson for Māori affairs, education, energy and conservation; stood for leader in 2014, finishing fourth. - **Sixth Labour Government:** Minister of Local Government (2017–2023) and Māori Development (2017–2020); **Minister of Foreign Affairs, 6 Nov 2020 – Nov 2023** — the first woman and first Māori woman in the role ([Stuff](https://stuff.co.nz/national/politics/123271205/nanaia-mahuta-will-be-foreign-minister-and-the-first-woman-to-do-the-job)); Disarmament and Arms Control (2023). ## Record & notable actions - **Three Waters:** led the reform to move council water services into four large entities with council/mana whenua co-governance; the Water Services Entities Act passed on 7 December 2022 with only Labour's votes. She later acknowledged underestimating public opposition and problems with the advertising campaign ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2022/03/13/mahuta-admits-getting-things-wrong-with-three-waters-reform/); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/130704446/labour-alone-in-support-of-three-waters-bill-as-it-passes-into-law)). The reforms were restructured under Hipkins in 2023 and repealed by the National-led government's Water Services Acts Repeal Act 2024 ([Wikipedia: Three Waters reform programme](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Waters_reform_programme)). - **Māori wards:** passed the Local Electoral (Māori Wards and Māori Constituencies) Amendment Act 2021, removing the ability of local polls to overturn council decisions to create Māori wards ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/437105/maori-wards-amendment-bill-passes-final-reading-in-parliament)). - **Foreign policy:** introduced the Russia Sanctions Act 2022 (passed unanimously on 9 March 2022); suspended high-level contact with Myanmar after the 2021 coup; joined Five Eyes statements on Hong Kong while saying New Zealand would not let Five Eyes dictate its China relationship (April 2021) ([Al Jazeera](https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2021/4/19/new-zealand-says-it-will-set-china-policy-not-us-led-five-eyes)). - Commissioned the Future for Local Government review (2021–2023) and appointed commissioners to run Tauranga City Council (2020), later extended to 2024. - **Conscience votes:** voted against the Abortion Legislation Act 2020 (but for safe-areas legislation in 2022); in 2004 voted against her party's foreshore and seabed bill at first and second reading, then for it at third reading. ## Controversies - **Tauranga commissioners:** legal reviews commissioned by critics argued her decisions to install and then extend commissioners may have been unlawful; Local Government NZ's president called the extension "disgusting" ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/463183/tauranga-city-commissioners-retained-until-july-2024-minister-says)). - **Family contracts (2022):** National questioned government contracts awarded to her husband's company and relatives; a Public Service Commission review found agencies had not properly managed conflicts but found "no evidence of favouritism, bias, or undue influence" ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/business/public-service-commission-finds-govt-agencies-were-substandard-in-their-processes-signing-contracts-with-companies-of-family-members-of-nanaia-mahuta/XAUV7FJUXJEWRGL72BRKC5NNJE/)). - **Entrenchment clause (Dec 2022):** supported a Green amendment entrenching water-asset ownership against Cabinet's position; Christopher Luxon called for her sacking, while Ardern defended her ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/480290/christopher-luxon-calls-for-nanaia-mahuta-to-be-sacked-over-entrenchment-clause)). - **7 October 2023 statement:** her initial statement on the Hamas attack, which called for a halt to violence without condemning Hamas, was criticised; she later said she had rejected MFAT advice to use stronger language ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/11/19/nanaia-mahuta-on-israel-gaza-tweet-cant-dwell-on-mistakes/)). - ACT criticised her limited overseas travel as foreign minister (2022) ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/australias-foreign-minister-penny-wong-putting-nanaia-mahuta-to-shame-with-solomons-trip-act/M4UFDB5MY2ICPY7BDR7WFSIUQQ/)). ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - 3rd Minister for Whānau Ora (2017–2023) | | **Wikipedia** | [Peeni Henare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peeni_Henare) | ## Current status Henare announced on 3 February 2026 that he would not seek the Tāmaki Makaurau nomination or a list place and would leave Parliament; his resignation took effect on 15 March 2026 and Dan Rosewarne took his list seat ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/waitangi-2026-senior-labour-mp-peeni-henare-leaving-the-party-report/ZAWGQIRAHNHCPMZZW6CXCSKTWY/); [NZ Gazette](https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2026-ps1387)). In his valedictory speech he urged MPs to move away from "gotcha-style politics" ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/589302/peeni-henare-tells-mps-to-move-away-from-gotcha-style-politics-in-valedictory-speech)). In July 2026 New Zealand Rugby appointed him Kaihautū Māori ([Te Ao Māori News](https://www.teaonews.co.nz/2026/07/23/former-minister-peeni-henare-appointed-kaihautu-maori-for-new-zealand-rugby/)). ## Biography Henare (Ngāti Hine) is a great-grandson of Taurekareka Hēnare (MP for Northern Maori 1914–1938) and son of Māori Language Commission head Erima Henare; former MP Tau Henare is his second cousin ([Northern Advocate](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/northern-advocate/news/grandson-aims-to-keep-parliament-seat-in-family/BTMULIR4F6LCJ3EGMT6DSKINIE/)). His partner is Skye Kimura, former chief executive of consultancy Tātou. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 51st | 2014–2017 | Tāmaki Makaurau | none | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Tāmaki Makaurau | none | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Tāmaki Makaurau | 18 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–2026 | List | 14 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 41st Minister of Defence | 6 November 2020 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 38th Minister of Tourism | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 32nd Minister of Forestry | 12 April 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 14th Minister for Youth | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 16th Minister for ACC | 1 February 2023 | 27 November 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 3rd Minister for Whānau Ora | 26 October 2017 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 26th Minister of Civil Defence | 27 June 2019 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 8th Minister for the Community and Voluntary Sector | 26 October 2017 | 3 July 2019 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **Tāmaki Makaurau MP 2014–2023:** won in 2014; held it in 2017 and narrowly in 2020 (927 after a recount requested by Te Pāti Māori's John Tamihere); lost it in 2023 to Te Pāti Māori's Takutai Tarsh Kemp by 42 votes (confirmed by a judicial recount) and returned on the list ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/11/15/takutai-kemp-extends-lead-in-tamaki-makaurau-recount/)). Lost the September 2025 Tāmaki Makaurau by-election (after Kemp's death) to Te Pāti Māori's Oriini Kaipara, 3,093 votes to 6,031 on preliminary results ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/09/06/oriini-kaipara-wins-tamaki-makaurau-byelection/)). - **Minister 2017–2023:** Whānau Ora (2017–2023), Civil Defence (2019–2020), Defence (2020–2023, in Cabinet), associate health (Māori), housing and tourism; from January 2023 ACC, Tourism and Environment ([DPMC 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf)). - **Opposition:** defence, sport, associate health; later economic development and Māori–Crown relations, and briefly foreign affairs after David Parker's retirement (2025). ## Record & notable actions - In November 2022 became the first New Zealand Cabinet minister to visit Ukraine after the Russian invasion ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/peeni-henare-becomes-first-minister-to-visit-ukraine-since-conflict/PBWO6GRR7BE5ROICB6PNK5MI4Y/)). - Member's bill to ban imports made with slave labour (defeated at first reading, 2016). ## Controversies - **Tātou contracts (2023):** National sought a review of about $600,000 of government contracts awarded to his partner's firm; Henare had declared the interest in 2018. A 2024 PwC review found the Ministry of Health had not properly managed conflicts of interest on its contracts ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/508184/health-ministry-admits-failings-in-handling-contracts-it-awarded-to-firm-with-links-to-peeni-henare)). - **"Gun" metaphor (Feb 2024):** a te reo speech line "I lift my gun, and I let the shots do the talking" drew ACT criticism; On 6 March 2025 Winston Peters dismissed him after he questioned, at a Chatham House event, whether Donald Trump understood history (invoking Churchill's criticism of the Munich Agreement); Luxon backed the decision, Hipkins said Goff had "overstepped the mark", and Helen Clark accused the government of placating the Trump administration ([Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/mar/06/phil-goff-donald-trump-comments-new-zealand-high-commissioner-removed-chatham-house-ntwnfb); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360604666/comment-cost-phil-goff-his-job-high-commissioner)). He later said he had "no regrets" ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/04/04/no-regrets-phil-goff-breaks-silence-on-trump-remark-sacking/)). ## Biography Born 22 June 1953 and raised in Three Kings, Auckland, Goff left home at 16 to attend university, working at a freezing works and as a cleaner to gain an MA (first-class honours) in political studies at the University of Auckland; he later organised for the Insurance Workers Union ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/general/candidate-profile-phil-goff-2011100311)). Chris Hipkins; Christopher Luxon | | 2nd Mayor of Auckland | 15 October 2016 | 15 October 2022 | | | 32nd Leader of the Opposition | 19 November 2008 | 13 December 2011 | John Key | | 13th Leader of the Labour Party | 11 November 2008 | 13 December 2011 | | | 35th Minister of Defence | 19 October 2005 | 19 November 2008 | Helen Clark | | 25th Minister of Foreign Affairs | 10 December 1999 | 19 October 2005 | Helen Clark | | 43rd Minister of Justice | 10 December 1999 | 19 October 2005 | Helen Clark | | 37th Minister of Education | 14 August 1989 | 2 November 1990 | Geoffrey Palmer ; Mike Moore | | 9th Minister of Employment | 6 April 1987 | 14 August 1989 | David Lange | | 14th Minister of Housing | 26 July 1984 | 26 August 1987 | David Lange | | Member of the New Zealand Parliament | 6 November 1993 | 12 October 2016 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - **MP for Roskill/Mt Roskill 1981–1990 and 1993–2016.** Youngest member of David Lange's 1984 Cabinet (Housing, Environment, later Employment, Tertiary Education and Education). - **Fifth Labour Government:** Minister of Foreign Affairs and Trade and Justice (1999–2005); Defence, Trade, Disarmament and Pacific Island Affairs, and Associate Finance (2005–2008). - **Labour leader and Leader of the Opposition, 11 Nov 2008 – 13 Dec 2011**; Labour fell to 27.5% in 2011 and he stood down. Later spokesperson for foreign affairs, then defence and Auckland. - Resigned from Parliament on 12 October 2016 after winning the Auckland mayoralty, triggering the Mt Roskill by-election won by Michael Wood ([NZ Gazette](https://www.gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2016-ps5847)). ## Record & notable actions - Signed the New Zealand–China Free Trade Agreement in Beijing on 7 April 2008 ([Stuff](http://www.stuff.co.nz/4466946a27013.html)); involved in the 2001 decision to accept 131 Tampa refugees. - Introduced student fees and loans as tertiary education minister (late 1980s). - As opposition leader campaigned against raising GST to 15% and against mining on conservation land (2010). - As Auckland mayor (2016–2022) barred far-right speakers Lauren Southern and Stefan Molyneux from council venues (2018), prompting a free-speech legal challenge that was withdrawn ([RNZ](https://www.radionz.co.nz/news/national/362611/free-speech-coalition-withdraws-urgent-legal-action-over-goff-s-southern-molyneux-decision)), and opposed the Three Waters mandate (2021). ## Controversies - **SFO inquiry (2020–2022):** the Serious Fraud Office investigated his 2016 mayoral campaign's declaration of auction donations; it closed the inquiry in April 2022 with no charges ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/464825/sfo-ends-two-year-probe-of-donations-to-auckland-mayor-s-election-campaigns)). - **Coronation remarks (2023):** apologised after offending Kiingi Tūheitia's delegation in London by forgetting a karakia and saying no one present had experienced a coronation ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/489302/high-commissioner-to-the-uk-phil-goff-offends-maori-king-with-coronation-comments-forgotten-karakia)). - **Trump remarks and dismissal (2025):** see Current status. ## 2026 candidacy Not listed as a Labour candidate for the 2026 election on policy.nz (Oct 2026). ## Sources - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phil_Goff - https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/mar/06/phil-goff-donald-trump-comments-new-zealand-high-commissioner-removed-chatham-house-ntwnfb - https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360604666/comment-cost-phil-goff-his-job-high-commissioner - https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/04/04/no-regrets-phil-goff-breaks-silence-on-trump-remark-sacking/ - https://www.newshub.co.nz/general/candidate-profile-phil-goff-2011100311 - https://www.gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2016-ps5847 - http://www.stuff.co.nz/4466946a27013.html - https://www.radionz.co.nz/news/national/362611/free-speech-coalition-withdraws-urgent-legal-action-over-goff-s-southern-molyneux-decision - https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/464825/sfo-ends-two-year-probe-of-donations-to-auckland-mayor-s-election-campaigns - https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/489302/high-commissioner-to-the-uk-phil-goff-offends-maori-king-with-coronation-comments-forgotten-karakia _Profile compiled 2026-10-23 from the sources above; chair of the Finance and Expenditure Committee; **Minister for Building and Construction** (Oct 2007 – Nov 2008) with associate Treaty negotiations, immigration and trade roles. - Opposition spokesperson for economic development, fisheries, Māori affairs and other portfolios; stood for Labour leader in 2013, winning 7 of 34 caucus votes ([Stuff](http://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/9166765/Cunliffe-wins-Labour-leadership)). - Resigned from Parliament in May 2014 to become Pacific Economic Ambassador under National's Murray McCully; Kelvin Davis took his list seat ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/news/article.cfm?c_id=1&objectid=11242350)). - Rejoined Parliament for NZ First in 2017 (Minister for Regional Economic Development and Forestry, running the $3b Provincial Growth Fund), lost his seat in 2020, returned in 2023. ## Controversies (Labour era) - **Credit card (2010):** demoted after it emerged he had used a ministerial credit card for personal spending, including hotel pay-per-view adult films, which he had repaid ([NZ Herald](http://www.nzherald.co.nz/politics/news/article.cfm?c_id=280&objectid=10651965)). - **Bill Liu (Yong Ming Yan) citizenship (2008/2012):** stood down from Labour's front bench in 2012 over his 2008 decision, against officials' advice, to grant citizenship to Labour donor William Yan; the Auditor-General found no improper motive or political interference ([OAG report](https://oag.parliament.nz/2013/citizenship/docs/inquiry-citizenship.pdf/view)). - **Countdown allegations (2014):** accused Progressive Enterprises of extortion of suppliers; After he said National MP Katie Nimon had been "lazy" for taking parental leave, Christopher Luxon said Nash would not be a minister in any government he led, and NZ First accepted Nash's resignation as a candidate on 22 July 2026; he later apologised to Nimon ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/772673/significant-distraction-stuart-nash-resigns-as-nz-first-candidate-after-sexist-comments)). In September 2025 he had resigned from his job at recruiter Robert Walters and from the Taxpayers' Union board after a crude on-air definition of a woman on The Platform ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/572769/former-labour-mp-stuart-nash-resigns-after-comment-about-women)). ## Biography Born in August 1967 and adopted by Jenny and Hal Nash — making him the adoptive great-grandson of Prime Minister Sir Walter Nash — he grew up in Napier, attended Napier Boys' High School, and gained master's degrees in law, forestry science and management from the University of Canterbury before working at AUT ([Parliament profile](https://www3.parliament.nz/en/mps-and-electorates/former-members-of-parliament/nash-stuart/)). He is married to Sarah Nash and has four children. ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 49th | 2008–2011 | List | 36 | Labour | | 51st | 2014–2017 | Napier | none | Labour | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | Napier | 11 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | Napier | 12 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 9th Minister for Economic Development | 1 February 2023 | 28 March 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 32nd Minister of Forestry | 6 November 2020 | 28 March 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 11th Minister for Oceans and Fisheries | 1 February 2023 | 28 March 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 39th Minister of Police | 1 February 2023 | 15 March 2023 | Chris Hipkins | | 9th Minister for Economic and Regional Development | 6 November 2020 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 37th Minister of Tourism | 6 November 2020 | 1 February 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 11th Minister of Fisheries | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 30th Minister of Revenue | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Career summary - Contested Epsom for Labour in 2005; **list MP 2008–2011**; lost Napier to Chris Tremain in 2011 and briefly served as chief of staff to Labour leader David Shearer. - **Napier MP 2014–2023:** won with a 3,850 majority in 2014 (aided by Conservative Garth McVicar splitting the right vote), increased it in 2017, and held it by 5,856 in 2020 ([2014](http://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2014/electorate-29.html); [2020](https://www.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2020/electorate-details-26.html)). - **Minister 2017–2023:** Police, Revenue, Small Business and Fisheries (2017–2020); Economic and Regional Development, Forestry, Tourism and Small Business (2020–2023); Police again (2023) until his resignation from that portfolio in March 2023 ([DPMC 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf)). ## Controversies - **Police independence (March 2023):** resigned as Police Minister after disclosing he had phoned the Police Commissioner urging an appeal of a sentence he considered too light ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/486012/stuart-nash-has-resigned-as-police-minister-pm-hipkins-says)). It then emerged the Attorney-General had reprimanded him in 2020 for comments about a murder accused before trial, and that he had lobbied MBIE for a constituent; Hipkins demoted him to the bottom of Cabinet on a "final warning" ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/486178/stuart-nash-demoted-to-bottom-of-cabinet-now-on-his-final-warning-hipkins)). - **Dismissal (28 March 2023):** sacked from all portfolios after it was revealed he had emailed two donors in 2020 about confidential Cabinet discussions on commercial rent relief ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131627166/stuart-nash-sacked-as-minister-after-email-to-donors-emerged)). A Cabinet Office review in June 2023 found no further confidentiality breaches but identified an unmanaged conflict of interest over the appointment of donor Phil McCaw; the Chief Ombudsman found he had breached the Official Information Act by withholding the donor emails ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/492084/stuart-nash-did-not-share-confidential-information-with-other-donors-probe-finds); [Newsroom](https://www.newsroom.co.nz/stuart-nash-breached-official-information-laws-ombudsman)). He announced on 3 April 2023 that he would not stand again. - **Groundswell remarks (2021):** said the farmer protest group's website promoted racism and vaccine hesitancy, which its organisers rejected ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/127032009/nash-says-groundswell-stands-for-racist-antivax-sentiment)). - **Post-politics:** criticised Labour's gang-asset law as too weak and alleged Kiri Allan had blocked tougher measures (2024); Willie Jackson accused him of grandstanding ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/510204/stuart-nash-claims-labour-cabinet-softened-its-gang-asset-seizure-policy)). 3rd Leader of Mana Motuhake (2001–2003) | | **Wikipedia** | [Willie Jackson (politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willie_Jackson_%28politician%29) | ## Current status Jackson is No. 4 on Labour's 2026 list (list-only) ([policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/labour-party)) and, since the 11 March 2026 reshuffle, Labour's spokesperson for Māori development, Māori–Crown relations and associate health (Māori) ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360949687/hipkins-reshuffles-labour-portfolios-henare-departs-and-plan-hatched-maori-seats-race)). He has again led Labour's campaign for the Māori electorates; Labour won only one of the seven in 2023, after which he said he had considered quitting ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/senior-mp-willie-jackson-to-leave-politics-following-hefty-defeat-at-the-polls-but-only-if-hes-not-wanted/MTUJK4PQDJBKFNX7PZNZOCAPLY/)). ## Biography Born in 1961 (Ngāti Maniapoto, Ngāti Porou), the son of urban Māori leaders Dame June Jackson and Bob Jackson; his uncles included activist Syd Jackson and lawyer Moana Jackson ([The Spinoff](https://thespinoff.co.nz/atea/28-02-2019/the-incredible-legacy-of-dame-june-jackson)). After leaving Māngere College he became a freezing worker and, at 21, president of the freezing workers' union. In the 1990s he ran Tangata Records and managed Moana and the Moahunters. A broadcaster for two decades, he ran Radio Waatea and Urban Māori Broadcasting, hosted *Eye to Eye* (TV One, 2004–2009) and talkback on RadioLive with John Tamihere. He chaired the National Urban Māori Authority (from 2003) and led the Manukau Urban Māori Authority (from 2009), whose subsidiary won a charter-school contract in 2017 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/kahu/labour-candidate-willie-jackson-benefits-from-new-round-of-charter-schools/G676BTHOOKBLSAFRVUKYOFEZKE/)). ## Political career ### Parliamentary terms | Parliament | Years | Electorate | List position | Party | |---|---|---|---|---| | 46th | 1999–2002 | List | 9 | Alliance (New Zealand political party) | | 52nd | 2017–2020 | List | 22 | Labour | | 53rd | 2020–2023 | List | 19 | Labour | | 54th | 2023–present | List | 9 | Labour | _Source: Wikipedia parliamentary-term table._ ### Offices held | Office | From | To | Prime Minister at the time | |---|---|---|---| | 27th Minister of Broadcasting and Media | 14 June 2022 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 45th Minister for Māori Development | 6 November 2020 | 27 November 2023 | Jacinda Ardern; Chris Hipkins | | 17th Minister of Employment | 26 October 2017 | 6 November 2020 | Jacinda Ardern | | 3rd Leader of Mana Motuhake | 2 June 2001 | 4 December 2003 | | _Source: Wikipedia infobox._ ### Opposition portfolios (as of 11 March 2026) Rank 5 in Chris Hipkins' shadow cabinet: - Spokesperson for Māori Development - Spokesperson for Māori Crown Relations - Associate Spokesperson for Health (Māori) _Source: [Shadow Cabinet of Chris Hipkins](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shadow_Cabinet_of_Chris_Hipkins), list as of 11 March 2026._ ### Career summary - **Alliance MP, 1999–2002** (Mana Motuhake); led Mana Motuhake from 2001 and was Alliance deputy leader at the 2002 election, when the party lost all its seats. - **Labour list MP, 2017–present.** Recruited by Andrew Little to run Labour's Māori-seat campaign in 2017, when Labour won all seven Māori electorates ([RNZ](http://www.radionz.co.nz/news/political/323829/willie-jackson-to-stand-for-labour)). - **Minister:** Minister of Employment (outside Cabinet) and Associate Minister for Māori Development, 2017–2020; Minister for Māori Development in Cabinet from November 2020, plus associate ACC and justice; Minister of Broadcasting and Media from June 2022 ([DPMC 2020](https://dpmc.govt.nz/sites/default/files/2020-11/ministerial-list-2-nov-2020.pdf)); co-chair of Labour's Māori caucus. - **Opposition:** Māori development, broadcasting, employment and associate portfolios (2023); Māori development and social development (March 2025); Māori development, Māori–Crown relations and associate health (Māori) (March 2026). ## Record & notable actions - **Public media merger:** introduced the Aotearoa New Zealand Public Media Bill to merge RNZ and TVNZ (2022); it was scrapped by the Hipkins government in February 2023 ([Parliament](https://www.parliament.nz/en/pb/bills-and-laws/bills-proposed-laws/document/BILL_125298/aotearoa-new-zealand-public-media-bill); [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/131174007/rnztvnz-merger-gone-minimum-wage-rises-policies-delayed-in-government-refocus)). - Apologised to Moriori on behalf of Ngāti Tama and Ngāti Mutunga as the Moriori Claims Settlement passed in 2021 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/moriori-praised-for-dedication-patience-as-18m-and-apology-settlement-with-crown-becomes-law/VR32NHE6MDBEHZE6ZL5Z2X5NDU/)). - A leading opponent of ACT's Treaty Principles Bill; won a 2024 Oxford Union debate calling for the return of mokomōkai from the British Museum ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2024/05/24/willie-jackson-calls-for-return-of-mokomokai-in-oxford-debate-win/)). ## Controversies - **Roast Busters interview (2013):** he and John Tamihere were taken off air at RadioLive after an interview with a friend of an alleged victim in which the group's actions were described as "mischief" ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/roast-busters-radiolive-hosts-taken-off-air/C4HJSTJI55U546Q2OUS4OA7WUY/?c_id=1&objectid=11155132)). - **Jack Tame interview (Dec 2022):** a combative Q+A interview on the media merger, in which he questioned the host's motives, drew criticism including from Ardern; he gave a partial apology ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/480223/willie-jackson-gives-partial-apology-over-public-media-merger-interview)). - **"Go to war" remark (Nov 2023):** said Māori would "go to war" if the incoming government pursued a Treaty principles referendum; ACT leader David Seymour responded that people who "threaten war" instead of debate "are not being a good actor" ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2023/11/labour-mp-willie-jackson-warns-of-m-ori-uprising-over-act-s-proposed-treaty-referendum.html)). - **Ejections from the House:** in December 2021 (refusing to withdraw calling ACT "right-wing fascists"), November 2024 (calling David Seymour a liar during the Treaty Principles Bill first reading) and May 2025 ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/politics/maori-development-minister-willie-jackson-kicked-out-of-parliament-for-right-wing-fascist-comment/OIZQJ3QM42VSM3GSSLE7YLLIYY/); [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/533792/watch-labour-s-willie-jackson-ejected-from-house-for-calling-david-seymour-a-liar-during-treaty-principles-bill-reading); [1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/05/15/labours-willie-jackson-booted-from-house/)). ## 2026 candidacy - She was selected on 5 February 2026 to contest the Māori electorate of Te Tai Tokerau, held by Te Pāti Māori's Mariameno Kapa-Kingi ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/360931874/greens-labour-and-te-pati-maori-gear-intense-te-tai-tokerau-battle)). She holds BA, LLB, PGDip and LLM degrees from the University of Waikato and worked as a solicitor in Wellington before returning north ([Waikato University](http://www.waikato.ac.nz/study/success-stories/willow-jean-prime)). Led the Mana Movement until May 2021. Not a 2026 candidate. ## Biography Born in Whangārei on 6 January 1955 to John and Titewhai Harawira (a prominent activist); of Ngāti Hau, Ngāti Wai, Ngāti Hine, Te Aupōuri, Ngāpuhi and Ngāti Whātua descent. Raised in West Auckland; attended St Stephen's School and the University of Auckland. A long-time activist — He Taua (1979), the 1981 Springbok tour protests, land occupations, Māori language and broadcasting, and the 2004 foreshore and seabed hīkoi. Married to Hilda Halkyard-Harawira. ## Political career - Won **Te Tai Tokerau** for the Māori Party in 2005 and 2008. - Clashed with the party over its support for the National-led government and the foreshore and seabed replacement law; suspended from caucus and left the party in February 2011. - Founded the **Mana Party** (April 2011), resigned to force a by-election and won it (June 2011, majority 1,117); re-elected in November 2011. - In 2014 Mana ran jointly with Kim Dotcom's Internet Party; Harawira lost to Labour's Kelvin Davis after National and NZ First urged tactical votes for Davis. Lost again to Davis in 2017. ## Record & notable actions - **"Feed the Kids" Bill** (Education (Breakfast and Lunch Programmes in Schools) Amendment Bill, drawn 2012): free meals in decile 1–2 schools — a forerunner of later school-lunch policy. - Arrested in 2012 at a Glen Innes state-house demolition protest; organised free breakfasts in South Auckland. - Led iwi COVID-19 checkpoints into the Far North in 2020–21 (some shut down by police). ## Controversies - A long record of inflammatory remarks: a 2009 profane email to Buddy Mikaere about "white motherf***ers" after skipping a European conference for Paris (he apologised for the wording, not the sentiment); calling John Howard a "racist bastard"; describing National's Māori MPs as John Key's "little house niggers" (2012); praising Osama bin Laden as a man who "fought for... his people" (2011, later apologised for how he expressed it); and in 2017 calling for the death penalty for Chinese methamphetamine importers. - Said in 2010 he "wouldn't feel comfortable" if his children brought home a Pākehā partner. ## Sources - https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Hone_Harawira&oldid=1363715231 - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_P%C4%81ti_M%C4%81ori

# Andrew Falloon

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |

| **Parliaments** | 52nd |
| **First elected** | 2017 |
| **Born** | 1983-08-29 — Ashburton, New Zealand |
| **Wikipedia** | [Andrew Falloon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andrew_Falloon) |

## Current status

Former MP. He resigned on 21 July 2020 (see Controversies). His activities since are not detailed in the sources consulted.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born on 29 August 1983 in Ashburton. He boarded at Christchurch Boys' High School and studied political science and economics at the University of Canterbury.
- **Early politics:** stood list-only for ACT in 2005 and 2008.
- **Parliamentary staff:** from 2007, a parliamentary researcher, then a staffer in the offices of Rodney Hide, Phil Heatley and Steven Joyce.

## Political career

- **Rangitata (2017):** won the seat for National, beating Labour's Jo Luxton by 6,331 votes.
- **Spokesperson:** South Island regional development under Simon Bridges, then biosecurity under Todd Muller and Judith Collins.

**Roles held:**

- MP for Rangitata (2017–2020)
- National spokesperson for biosecurity; South Island regional development

## Record & notable actions

- **Conscience votes:** a social liberal; voted for the End of Life Choice and abortion bills.

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [End of Life Choice Bill — third reading, 13 Nov 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Life_Choice_Act_2019) | for |
| [Abortion Legislation Bill — third reading, 18 Mar 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020) | for |

## Controversies

- **Resignation (July 2020):**
  - On 20 July 2020 he announced he would not seek re-election, citing personal reasons.
  - It was then reported that he had sent a pornographic image to a 19-year-old student. He claimed someone else had used his phone.
  - Judith Collins said she "no longer trusted his story" after reports of further explicit messages to other women, and he resigned effective immediately on 21 July.
  - At least five women reported similar behaviour. Police investigated but did not lay charges.

# Cam Calder

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |
| **Now (Oct 2026)** | Retired from Parliament at the 2014 election. Has since acted as a Commonwealth election observer (Sri Lanka, 2015) and written opinion pieces (NZ Herald, 2021). |
| **Electorate(s)** | List MP (2009–2014); contested Manurewa 2008, 2011 |
| **Parliaments** | 49th, 50th |
| **First elected** | 2009 (list vacancy) |
| **Born** | 1952 |
| **Wikipedia** | [Cam Calder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cam_Calder) |

## Current status

Former MP. He retired at the 2014 election, and Simeon Brown replaced him as National's Manurewa candidate. He was a Commonwealth election observer in Sri Lanka in 2015. In 2021 he wrote a NZ Herald op-ed criticising the new NZ history curriculum.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born in 1952 and raised in New Plymouth.
- **Medicine:** trained as a dentist at Otago, then retrained in medicine at Cambridge. He worked as an emergency doctor in England and New Zealand, and later as clinical research director for an equipment company.
- **Other interests:** president of the French New Zealand Business Council and a pétanque promoter; he represented New Zealand at the 1995 world championships.
- **Personal:** married to Jenny; two children.

## Political career

- **Joined National:** 2003.
- **2008:** contested Manurewa (#58 on the list) and missed out when the final count cut National's seats by one.
- **List MP (June 2009):** entered Parliament when Richard Worth resigned, and was re-elected on the list in 2011.
- **Committees:** chaired the Education and Science Committee (2013–14); deputy chair of the Justice and Electoral Committee.

**Roles held:**

- List MP (2009–2014)
- Chair, Education and Science Committee (2013–2014)

## Record & notable actions

- **Laser pointers:** his member's bill restricting high-powered laser pointers in public places became law in July 2014.
- **Conscience votes:** voted for marriage equality (2013) and supported raising the alcohol purchase age to 20.

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill — third reading, 17 Apr 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Definition_of_Marriage)_Amendment_Act_2013) | for |

## Controversies

None significant identified in the sources consulted.

# Chris Auchinvole

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |
| **Now (Oct 2026)** | Retired at the 2014 election. According to Wikipedia he farms Highland cattle on the West Coast with his wife (unverified recent status). |

| **Born** | 1945-03-07 — Prestwick, Ayrshire, Scotland |
| **Wikipedia** | [Chris Auchinvole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Auchinvole) |

## Current status

Former MP. He retired at the 2014 election, and Maureen Pugh replaced him as National's West Coast-Tasman candidate. According to Wikipedia he and his wife farm Highland cattle near Lake Brunner.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born on 7 March 1945 in Prestwick, Scotland. He attended Sandhurst.
- **New Zealand:** naturalised in 1980. He worked in exporting on the West Coast.
- **Other roles:** Uniting Church lay preacher and wedding celebrant.

## Political career

- **List MP (2005):** entered Parliament on the list after losing West Coast-Tasman.
- **West Coast-Tasman (2008):** won the seat from Labour's Damien O'Connor.
- **2011:** lost the seat back to O'Connor but was returned on the list.
- **Retirement:** announced in October 2013.

**Roles held:**

- MP for West Coast-Tasman (2008–2011)
- List MP (2005–2008, 2011–2014)

## Record & notable actions

- **Marriage equality:** a strong supporter of the 2013 bill; his second-reading speech was widely praised.
- **Celebrant:** officiated at Tau Henare's wedding in Parliament (2012).

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill — third reading, 17 Apr 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Definition_of_Marriage)_Amendment_Act_2013) | for |

## Controversies

None significant identified in the sources consulted.

He is National's leader (since 30 November 2021) and MP for Botany (since 2020), and heads National's 2026 list at #1 while re-contesting Botany. 2026 has been turbulent for his leadership. On 12 August 2026, at an emergency caucus meeting, he again won a confidence vote, this time against a challenge from Defence Minister Chris Penk. Luxon then stripped Penk of his portfolios, and Penk withdrew from the election. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/592984/prime-minister-christopher-luxon-survives-confidence-vote), [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/975747/chris-penk-says-he-will-not-seek-re-election-after-losing-ministerial-portfolios), [Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/politics/361019447/how-nationals-secret-vote-works-after-chris-penks-failed-leadership-bid)) ## Biography - Born on 19 July 1970 in Christchurch and raised in a Catholic family.
