He earned a Master of Commerce from the University of Canterbury (1989–92). - **Unilever (1993–2011):** he started as a management trainee in Wellington and then worked in Sydney, London and Chicago. In 2008 he became president and CEO of Unilever Canada. - **Air New Zealand (2011–2019):** he joined as group general manager in 2011 and was named CEO in June 2012, taking over at the end of that year and serving until 2019. The airline posted record profits in that time, helped by a tourism boom, cuts to under-performing regional routes and job cuts. He sat on the board of Virgin Australia from 2014 to 2016, while Air NZ held a stake. In 2015 he was named Deloitte Top 200 CEO of the Year. - He describes himself as an evangelical/non-denominational Christian and has said "my faith is personal to me. It is not in itself a political agenda". He is married to Amanda, and they have two children. His declared wealth (March 2024) was estimated at NZ$21–30 million, including several properties. ## Political career - **2019:** selected for the safe National seat of Botany after Jami-Lee Ross left the party. ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/117151149/national-chooses-christopher-luxon-as-botany-mp)) - **2020 election:** won Botany with about 52% of the vote while National lost many seats. He was then spokesperson for local government, research, science, manufacturing and land information. - **30 Nov 2021:** became National leader unopposed after Judith Collins was removed and Simon Bridges withdrew, about a year after entering Parliament. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/456886/christopher-luxon-set-to-be-new-national-party-leader-as-simon-bridges-withdraws)) - **2023 election:** National won 38.1% of the party vote and 48 seats, and Luxon held Botany with about 67%. He signed separate coalition agreements with ACT and NZ First on 24 November 2023 and was sworn in on 27 November. ([DPMC](https://www.dpmc.govt.nz/publications/co-24-2-national-act-and-new-zealand-first-coalition-government-consultation-and-operating-arrangements)) - **Cabinet reshuffles:** - April 2024: Melissa Lee was removed from Cabinet, and Penny Simmonds lost the Disability Issues portfolio. - 19 January 2025: Simeon Brown took Health from Shane Reti, and Chris Bishop took Transport. - 2 April 2026: Penk entered Cabinet in Defence, Simmonds returned to Cabinet, and Bishop became Attorney-General but lost Leader of the House and campaign chair to Louise Upston and Simeon Brown. Media widely read the Bishop changes as linked to leadership tensions, which both men denied. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/515100/media-minister-melissa-lee-demoted-from-cabinet-penny-simmonds-stripped-of-portfolio), [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/539370/as-it-happened-luxon-announces-cabinet-reshuffle-shane-reti-loses-health-portfolio-to-simeon-brown), [Beehive](https://www.beehive.govt.nz/release/pm-refreshes-ministerial-team)) **Roles held:** - Prime Minister of New Zealand (2023–) - Minister for National Security and Intelligence (2023–) - Minister Responsible for Ministerial Services (2023–) - Leader of the National Party (2021–) - Leader of the Opposition (2021–2023) - MP for Botany (2020–) - National spokesperson for local government, research, science, manufacturing and land information (2020–2021) ## Record & notable actions As Prime Minister, the government he leads has done the following (see [`../../track-record.md`](../../track-record.md) for the party-level record): - **Economy and spending:** - Delivered the NZ$14.7b tax relief package in Budget 2024. - Made public-service savings. RNZ estimated about 9,500 public-sector roles were cut by May 2025. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/562350/how-many-public-sector-jobs-have-really-been-axed)) - The economy was in recession through 2024. Unemployment rose from 3.7% (June 2023) to about 5.2% (late 2025). - **Law and order:** - Reinstated "three strikes" sentencing. - Banned gang patches in public. - Piloted a military-style academy (boot camp) for serious young offenders. - Ended funding for section 27 cultural reports. - **Treaty and Māori policy:** - Supported ACT's Treaty Principles Bill to first reading only, as the coalition agreement required. National then voted it down. - Scaled back co-governance arrangements. - **Local government and water:** replaced Three Waters with "Local Water Done Well". - **Education:** with Erica Stanford, announced a new maths curriculum (2024) and the replacement of NCEA (announced August 2025). - **Abuse in care:** delivered the state's formal apology to survivors of abuse in state and faith-based care (November 2024). - **Welfare:** - Introduced a "traffic-light" sanctions regime for beneficiaries. - Required six-monthly Jobseeker reapplication. - Brought in parental-income testing for 18–19-year-olds (from November 2026). - **Foreign and defence policy:** - Moved closer to Five Eyes partners and showed interest in AUKUS Pillar II. - Announced NZ$12b of defence investment over four years (April 2025), aiming for about 2% of GDP. - Designated all of Hamas as a terrorist entity (2024). He later called Israel's conduct in Gaza "utterly, utterly appalling" (August 2025). - **Personal positions:** - He has said he is personally "pro-life", but that National would not change the Abortion Legislation Act 2020. - He voted for the Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Bill (2022) and gave National MPs a conscience vote on it. - He describes himself as a "soft republican". - He was not in Parliament for the 2013, 2019 and 2020 conscience votes. ## Controversies - **Accommodation allowance (2023–24):** he claimed about NZ$52,000 a year in accommodation support while living in his own Wellington apartment. After public criticism he stopped the claim and repaid it. - **Te reo lessons:** as Opposition leader he used taxpayer-funded te reo Māori lessons, while his government reviewed incentive payments for public servants to learn te reo. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/504994/christopher-luxon-s-reo-maori-lessons-paid-for-by-taxpayer)) - **Hawaii social-media post (2022):** a Facebook post implied he was in Te Puke while he was on holiday in Hawaii. He blamed a delay in his social-media team's updates. - **"Marmite sandwich" (March 2025):** his remark about the school-lunch programme drew criticism from principals and child-poverty advocates. - **Coalition management:** commentators and polls (e.g. April 2024) questioned how much control he has over his coalition partners, Seymour and Peters. - **Popularity:** he has had persistently low favourability. For example, an October 2025 poll found 27% viewed him positively and 51% unfavourably. ([The Post](https://www.thepost.co.nz/politics/360853311/big-names-risk-labour-pulls-ahead-and-christopher-luxon-loses-ground)) - **Mid-2026 "gaffes":** before the August 2026 confidence vote, media reported: - a "parent-child mentality" remark to Rotorua business leaders, for which he apologised; - an unconsulted pledge to hold an MMP referendum; - use of an NZDF jet after a party fundraiser. ## 2026 candidacy - **Electorate:** Botany - **List ranking:** 1 _Source: candidate questionnaire answers published on [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/national-party), retrieved Oct 2026._ ## Sources - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - Photo: — Supplied to policy.nz by the candidate/party (Not stated (candidate photo supplied to policy.nz; used for identification))

# Claudette Hauiti

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |
| **Now (Oct 2026)** | Left Parliament at the 2014 election. Returned to journalism; Radio Waatea's Parliamentary Press Gallery reporter (per Wikipedia). |

| **Parliaments** | 50th |
| **First elected** | 2013 (list vacancy) |
| **Born** | 1961-05-08 — Auckland, New Zealand |
| **Wikipedia** | [Claudette Hauiti](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudette_Hauiti) |

## Current status

Former MP and broadcaster. According to Wikipedia she reports for Radio Waatea from the Parliamentary Press Gallery, and she judged for the NZ International Film Festival in 2022.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born on 8 May 1961 in Auckland and raised in Mount Roskill. She is of Ngāti Porou, Te Whānau-ā-Apanui, Ngāpuhi, Ngāti Kuta and Ngāti Ruanui descent.
- **Education:** BA from Canberra College of Advanced Education.
- **Broadcasting:**
  - Founded the production company Front of the Box in 1993.
  - Executive producer and presenter of *Eye to Eye with Willie Jackson* (2004–09).
  - Produced the award-winning documentary *Children of the Revolution* (2008).
- **Personal:** civil union with Nadine Mau (2007); three children.

## Political career

- **2010:** stood for the Albert-Eden Local Board for Citizens & Ratepayers; not elected.
- **2011:** lost Māngere to William Sio.
- **List MP (May 2013):** replaced Aaron Gilmore as a list MP on 28 May 2013.
- **2014:** withdrew from the election in July, although already selected for Kelston. Chris Penk replaced her as the candidate.

**Roles held:**

- List MP (May 2013–2014)

## Record & notable actions

No significant legislative record in the sources consulted. She was not an MP for the 2013 marriage-equality vote.

## Controversies

- **Charge card (March 2014):** handed back her parliamentary charge card after using it for a Christmas trip to Australia.
- **Employing her wife (April 2014):** breached parliamentary rules by employing her wife in her office. She said she was unaware of the rule and ended the employment.
- **Spending after retiring:** reported to have spent about NZ$23,000 in expenses after announcing she would stand down.

## Sources

- <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claudette_Hauiti>

# David Bennett

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |
| **Now (Oct 2026)** | Retired at the 2023 election. Appointed to the board of Callaghan Innovation by Judith Collins in 2024; dairy farmer near Te Awamutu. |
| **Electorate(s)** | Hamilton East (2005–2020) |
| **Parliaments** | 48th, 49th, 50th, 51st, 52nd, 53rd |
| **First elected** | 2005 |
| **Born** | 1970-10-28 — Hamilton, New Zealand |
| **Wikipedia** | [David Bennett (New Zealand politician)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Bennett_(New_Zealand_politician)) |

## Current status

Former MP. He retired at the 2023 election to spend time with his family. In 2024 Science Minister Judith Collins appointed him to the board of Callaghan Innovation. ([NZ Gazette](https://gazette.govt.nz/notice/id/2024-go1520))

## Biography

- Born 28 October 1970 in Hamilton; attended St John's College.
- LLB and BCA from Victoria University of Wellington.
- Former KPMG accountant. Owns dairy farms near Te Awamutu.
- Formerly in a long-distance relationship with Australian Nationals senator Bridget McKenzie. He is now engaged to Nicky Preston, with whom he has a child.

## Political career

- **Hamilton East:** won the seat from Labour's Dianne Yates in 2005 and held it until 2020, when he lost to Jamie Strange by 2,973 votes. He then returned as a list MP until 2023.
- **Committee chair:** chaired the Transport and Finance select committees.
- **Ministerial roles:** Food Safety, Veterans' Affairs and Racing, outside Cabinet, under Bill English (2016–17). He was the first Hamilton MP to become a minister since 1984.

**Roles held:**

- Minister for Food Safety; Veterans' Affairs; Racing (2016–2017)
- Associate Minister of Transport (2016–2017)
- Chair, Finance and Expenditure Committee (2015–2017); Transport and Industrial Relations Committee (2011–2014)
- Assistant Speaker (2022)
- MP for Hamilton East (2005–2020)
- List MP (2020–2023)

## Record & notable actions

- **Marriage equality:** opposed the bill at first and second readings, then switched to support it at the third reading in 2013. He was the only MP recorded as changing to support.
- **Other conscience votes:**
  - Voted for the abortion bill at every stage.
  - Supported the abortion "safe areas" law and the 2022 conversion-practices ban.
  - Voted against the End of Life Choice Bill (see table).

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill — third reading, 17 Apr 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Definition_of_Marriage)_Amendment_Act_2013) | for |
| [End of Life Choice Bill — third reading, 13 Nov 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Life_Choice_Act_2019) | against |
| [Abortion Legislation Bill — third reading, 18 Mar 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020) | for |
| Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Bill — third reading, 15 Feb 2022 | not among the 8 National MPs recorded as opposed (25 National MPs voted in favour) |

## Controversies

- None of significance recorded in the sources consulted.

# Hamish Walker

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |
| **Now (Oct 2026)** | Did not stand in 2020 after the COVID-19 patient-data leak. Later worked in Queenstown real estate (Harcourts; then his own firm, since closed). |
| **Electorate(s)** | Clutha-Southland (2017–2020) |
| **Parliaments** | 52nd |
| **First elected** | 2017 |
| **Born** | 1985 — Dunedin, New Zealand |
| **Wikipedia** | [Hamish Walker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamish_Walker) |

## Current status

Former MP. He did not stand in 2020. He later sold real estate in Queenstown with Harcourts, then founded Premium Real Estate Queenstown, which has since closed.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born in 1985 and raised in Dunedin, where he attended John McGlashan College.
- **Diabetes:** diagnosed at 14.
- **Personal:** his family has roots in Balclutha. His wife, Penny Tipu, is of Māori descent.

## Political career

- **2014:** contested Dunedin South.
- **Clutha-Southland (2017):** a late replacement for Todd Barclay. He won by 14,354 votes.
- **Opposition roles:**
  - Associate agriculture spokesperson (2018–20).
  - Forestry and land information spokesperson (May–July 2020).
- **Local issues:** campaigned to keep Lumsden maternity services.

**Roles held:**

- MP for Clutha-Southland (2017–2020)
- National spokesperson for forestry and land information (May–Jul 2020)

## Record & notable actions

- **Conscience votes:** voted against the End of Life Choice and abortion bills.

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [End of Life Choice Bill — third reading, 13 Nov 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Life_Choice_Act_2019) | against |
| [Abortion Legislation Bill — third reading, 18 Mar 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020) | against |

## Controversies

- **Mataura post (Feb 2020):** admitted a social-media post falsely suggesting he had door-knocked in Mataura.
- **Quarantine statement (July 2020):** issued a press release objecting to quarantine facilities for returnees from India, Pakistan and South Korea. Ministers and Dunedin's mayor criticised it as racist "dog whistling", and Todd Muller reprimanded him.
- **Patient-data leak (July 2020):**
  - On 7 July he admitted leaking COVID-19 patient details to media, information he had received from former party president Michelle Boag. ([Stuff](https://www.stuff.co.nz/national/politics/300051710/national-mp-hamish-walker-admits-passing-on-leaked-covid19-patient-info-from-former-party-president-michelle-boag))
  - He was stripped of his portfolios, and Muller asked the party board to expel him. Walker announced he would not stand again. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/420754/covid-19-privacy-leak-mp-hamish-walker-announces-he-won-t-stand-for-re-election))
  - Michael Heron QC's inquiry found his actions were politically motivated and "not justified or reasonable".

## Sources

- <https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/420727/covid-19-privacy-leak-todd-muller-on-hamish-walker-there-needs-to-be-consequences>
- <https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/420754/covid-19-privacy-leak-mp-hamish-walker-announces-he-won-t-stand-for-re-election>

# Mike Sabin

| | |
|---|---|
| **Party** | New Zealand National Party |
| **Status** | Former MP |
| **Now (Oct 2026)** | Resigned from Parliament on 30 January 2015 'due to personal issues'; later reported working at Peppers Carrington Resort, Karikari (2015). Current activities not verified. |
| **Electorate(s)** | Northland (2011–2015) |
| **Parliaments** | 50th, 51st |
| **First elected** | 2011 |
| **Born** | 1968-09-24 |
| **Wikipedia** | [Mike Sabin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Sabin) |

## Current status

Former MP. He resigned on 30 January 2015, which triggered the 2015 Northland by-election; Winston Peters won it. In 2015 he was reported to be working at Peppers Carrington Resort in Karikari. His current activities are not verified.

## Biography

- **Early life:** born on 24 September 1968 and raised in Whangārei.
- **Navy and dairy:** seaman officer in the RNZ Navy in the 1980s, then worked in the dairy industry.
- **Police and drug education:**
  - Police officer from the 1990s.
  - Founded the drug-education company MethCon (2006; sold 2010).
  - Helped bring about the Alcohol and Other Drug Treatment Court.
  - Received a Sir Peter Blake Emerging Leader Award (2008).
- **Personal:** father of journalist Brook Sabin. He wrote *The Long Way Home*, about his son Darryl's rugby brain injury.

## Political career

- **Northland:** succeeded John Carter, winning by 11,362 votes in 2011 and 9,300 in 2014.
- **Ministerial prospects:** John Key later said he had considered making Sabin a minister after the 2014 election.

**Roles held:**

- MP for Northland (2011–2015)

## Record & notable actions

- **Conscience votes:** voted against marriage equality (2013).

**Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes):

| Bill | Vote |
|---|---|
| [Marriage (Definition of Marriage) Amendment Bill — third reading, 17 Apr 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marriage_(Definition_of_Marriage)_Amendment_Act_2013) | against |

## Controversies

- **Resignation (January 2015):** in December 2014 media reported he was under police investigation over an assault complaint. Police, Key and Sabin did not confirm the reports at the time. He resigned with immediate effect, citing personal issues "best dealt with outside Parliament".

## Sources

- <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Sabin>
- <http://www.scoop.co.nz/stories/PA1501/S00163/mike-sabin-announces-resignation-as-northland-mp.htm>

She has been deputy leader of the National Party since 30 November 2021. She is a list MP and is #2 on National's 2026 list without an electorate candidacy. She delivered Budget 2026 in late May 2026, forecasting a return to surplus (OBEGALx) by 2028/29 and ruling out "election-year band-aids and sugar hits". ([Treasury](https://www.treasury.govt.nz/publications/budget-speech/budget-speech-2026), [RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics/596610/budget-2026-at-a-glance-the-big-changes-winners-and-losers-what-you-need-to-know)) ## Biography - **Early life and education:** - Born on 7 March 1981 in Wellington and grew up in Point Howard, Lower Hutt. - Her mother was a Press Gallery journalist and her father a Bell Gully partner. Her great-great-grandfather Archibald Willis was a Liberal MP in the 1890s–1900s. - Attended Samuel Marsden Collegiate and King's College (Auckland). - Studied English literature at Victoria University of Wellington (first-class honours) and took a postgraduate journalism diploma at Canterbury. - **Early career:** research and policy adviser to Bill English, then senior adviser to John Key in 2008. During 2008 debate preparation she played Helen Clark. - **Business career:** - From 2012, government-relations manager and later general manager at Fonterra. - Board member of ExportNZ. - Director of the New Zealand Initiative (2016–17). - **Personal:** married to Duncan Small; four children. ([NZ Herald](https://www.nzherald.co.nz/nz/nicola-willis-at-home-who-is-nationals-new-deputy-leader-away-from-the-spotlight/C6R64EEY4CBSIOVW7BN5TETTTE/)) ## Political career - **2017 election:** contested Wellington Central and lost to Grant Robertson, taking about 26% of the electorate vote. She was #48 on the list and just missed out on the final count. - **3 April 2018:** entered Parliament from the list when Steven Joyce resigned. She was spokesperson for early childhood education. - **2020 leadership change:** worked as a "numbers" organiser, with Chris Bishop, in Todd Muller's successful challenge to Simon Bridges. She became housing spokesperson, and then education spokesperson under Judith Collins. - **2020 election:** lost Wellington Central again and returned on the list. As housing spokesperson she worked with Labour's Megan Woods on the cross-party Medium Density Residential Standards (2021). - **30 Nov 2021:** elected deputy leader unopposed as Christopher Luxon's running mate. She became finance spokesperson in March 2022 when Bridges resigned. - **2023 election:** lost Ōhāriu to Labour's Greg O'Connor by 1,260 votes; returned on the list. ([Electoral Commission](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-33.html)) - **Ministerial appointments:** - 27 Nov 2023: Finance, Public Service, Social Investment, Associate Climate Change. - January 2025: became the first Minister for Economic Growth and gave up the Public Service portfolio. **Roles held:** - Minister of Finance (2023–) - Minister for Social Investment (2023–) - Minister for Economic Growth (2025–) - Minister for the Public Service (2023–2025) - Associate Minister of Climate Change (2023–) - Acting Minister of Commerce and Consumer Affairs (Grocery Sector) (2025) - Deputy Leader of the National Party (2021–) - Deputy Leader of the Opposition (2021–2023) - National finance spokesperson (2022–2023) - National housing spokesperson (2020–2022) - National education spokesperson (2020) - List MP (2018–) ## Record & notable actions - **Fiscal stance:** - Mini-budget (20 Dec 2023): NZ$7.47b of claimed operating savings. - Budget 2024: about NZ$14b of personal income-tax relief, partly funded by public-service savings and programme cuts. - Budget 2025: reduced the new-spending allowance to NZ$1.3b and dropped the planned Digital Services Tax. - Budget 2026: focused on returning to surplus. - Treasury forecasts (Dec 2024) showed deficits until at least 2029. She adopted the OBEGALx measure, which excludes ACC, as the headline target. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/536933/hyefu-revealed-nicola-willis-deploys-convenient-new-measure-amid-bleak-books)) - **Interislander ferries:** - In December 2023 she declined KiwiRail's request for NZ$1.47b more for the iReX project, which ended it. Cancellation costs were put at about NZ$300m. - A replacement procurement through a new company was announced in December 2024, with new ships expected around 2029. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/504650/interislander-ferry-fleet-project-to-wind-down-after-being-denied-further-government-funding)) - **Cost of living and competition:** - Budget 2024 raised the Working for Families in-work tax credit, worth up to NZ$50 a fortnight for about 160,000 families. - Announced an "express lane" consenting regime (2025) to bring new supermarket competitors in. - In 2026 accused Foodstuffs and Woolworths of a "full-court press" lobbying campaign against reforms to break up the duopoly. ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/08/27/express-lane-reforms-to-increase-supermarket-competition-willis/)) - **Other decisions:** - Smallest minimum-wage rise since the 1990s, to NZ$23.50 (Dec 2024). - Guidance that public-service working from home is "not an entitlement" (Sept 2024). - Proposed relaxing government procurement rules, including the Living Wage requirement for cleaning and security contracts. - Announced a review of the Reserve Bank's COVID-era monetary policy (Feb 2026). - **Member's bill:** her 2023 bill to let parents share paid parental leave and take it at the same time was blocked by Labour at first reading. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/495025/labour-blocks-national-s-paid-parental-leave-bill-that-would-have-allowed-parents-to-share-time-off)) - **Positions:** - Described as a social liberal and a member of National's BlueGreens caucus. - Voted for the End of Life Choice and Abortion Legislation bills (see table). - Supported Labour's Equal Pay Amendment in 2018, but in 2025 backed the government bill restricting pay-equity claims, while calling herself a feminist. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/560142/pay-equity-changes-two-sides-of-the-coalition-brought-out)) **Conscience votes** (recorded third-reading votes): | Bill | Vote | |---|---| | [End of Life Choice Bill — third reading, 13 Nov 2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/End_of_Life_Choice_Act_2019) | for | | [Abortion Legislation Bill — third reading, 18 Mar 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion_Legislation_Act_2020) | for | | Conversion Practices Prohibition Legislation Bill — third reading, 15 Feb 2022 | not among the 8 National MPs recorded as opposed (25 National MPs voted in favour) | ## Controversies - **"$250 a fortnight" tax promise (2023):** - She admitted that only about 3,000 households would receive the full NZ$250 a fortnight. - She said she would resign if the tax plan was not delivered. - The foreign-buyer tax meant to help fund it was dropped in coalition talks. ([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2023/09/15/nicola-willis-id-quit-as-finance-minister-if-my-tax-cut-plan-fails/), [Newsroom](https://newsroom.co.nz/2023/11/24/which-policies-survived-the-negotiations-and-which-didnt/)) - **Cancer medicines (Budget 2024):** National's election promise to fund 13 cancer drugs was not met in Budget 2024. The government blamed a NZ$1.77b Pharmac funding "cliff" left by its predecessor, and Willis said the government would seek funding later. In June 2024 the government announced NZ$604m over four years for Pharmac to fund 54 medicines, including 26 cancer treatments, which it said fulfilled the promise ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/520419/cancer-drugs-promise-government-confirms-600m-extra-for-pharmac)). ([Newshub](https://www.newshub.co.nz/home/politics/2024/05/budget-2024-finance-minister-nicola-willis-defends-national-u-turn-on-funding-new-cancer-drugs.html)) - **Criticism of economic management:** - Open letters from 15 economists (Nov 2024) and 20 economists (Oct 2025) blamed fiscal restraint for prolonging the recession. Willis replied that she did not agree. - After a 0.9% GDP fall in the June 2025 quarter, Sir Roger Douglas and economist Robert MacCulloch called for her resignation. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/573459/former-finance-minister-sir-roger-douglas-calls-for-finance-minister-nicola-willis-to-resign)) - From the right, the Taxpayers' Union ran a "Nicola Fudge Co." campaign in December 2025. Willis challenged its chair, Ruth Richardson, to a debate, which did not go ahead. ## 2026 candidacy - **List ranking:** 2 _Source: candidate questionnaire answers published on [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/national-party), retrieved Oct 2026._ ## Sources - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - - Photo: — Supplied to policy.nz by the candidate/party (Not stated (candidate photo supplied to policy.nz; used for identification))

- **Committee chair:** Primary Production Committee (2008–14).

**Roles held:**

- Chair, Primary Production Committee (2008–2014)

## Record & notable actions

- **Fonterra:** a driving force behind the 2001 legislation that created Fonterra.
- **Conscience votes:** voted against marriage equality (2013).

([1News](https://www.1news.co.nz/2025/01/19/shane-reti-out-as-health-minister-as-pm-makes-major-cabinet-reshuffle/)) - **April 2026:** took back Energy and became campaign chair. **Roles held:** - Minister of Health (2025–) - Minister for State Owned Enterprises (2025–) - Minister for Energy (2023–2025, 2026–) - Minister for Auckland (2023–2026) - Minister of Transport (2023–2025) - Minister of Local Government (2023–2025) - Deputy Leader of the House (2023–) - Chair, National Party 2026 election campaign (2026–) - National spokesperson for police, corrections, youth, SFO (2020–2023); Auckland issues (2023) - MP for Pakuranga (2017–) - Manurewa Local Board member (2013–2017) ## Record & notable actions - **Transport (2023–25):** - Cancelled Auckland light rail and stopped the Transport Choices cycling and walking programme. - Reversed Labour's "blanket" speed-limit reductions through a new speed rule. - Made "New Zealand Transport Agency" the agency's primary name. - Put road-user charges on EVs and plug-in hybrids (April 2024). - Eased the Clean Car Standard. - Launched the NZ$32.9b 2024–27 National Land Transport Programme, including 17 Roads of National Significance and continued funding for the City Rail Link and Auckland busways. He has had type 1 diabetes since he was a toddler. - **Education:** Bachelor of Management Studies (accounting and finance) from the University of Waikato, and a Bachelor of Health Science (paramedicine) from AUT. - **Career:** - Chartered accountant. - Worked for the Royal Bank of Scotland in London during the 2008 financial crisis. - Deputy CFO of Waitematā DHB. - Front-line St John ambulance officer. - **Personal:** married with two sons. ## Political career - **2018:** lost the Northcote by-election selection to Dan Bidois. - **2020:** selected for North Shore and won by 3,734 votes. He was spokesperson for local government (a strong critic of Three Waters), climate change, ACC and other portfolios. His member's bill on ACC notices of decisions was defeated at first reading in 2021. - **2023:** held North Shore by 16,330 votes and became Minister of Climate Change and Revenue (outside Cabinet). He was promoted to Cabinet in April 2024. ([Electoral Commission](https://archive.electionresults.govt.nz/electionresults_2023/electorate-details-30.html)) **Roles held:** - Minister of Climate Change (2023–) - Minister of Revenue (2023–) - Minister of Local Government (2025–) - Minister for Energy (2025–2026) - Minister for Auckland (2026–) - Minister for Building and Construction (Aug 2026–) - National spokesperson for local government, regional development, ACC, climate change, statistics (2020–2023) - MP for North Shore (2020–) ## Record & notable actions **Climate** - Attended COP28 days after taking office and said New Zealand would advocate for a global fossil-fuel phase-out, while also reversing the oil-and-gas exploration ban. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/503501/new-climate-change-minister-simon-watts-not-expecting-criticism-at-cop28-over-fossil-fuels-u-turn)) - Released a five-pillar climate strategy and the second emissions reduction plan (2024). - Closed NZ Green Investment Finance (April 2025). ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/557556/government-s-green-investment-bank-to-be-shut-down)) - Withdrew New Zealand from the Beyond Oil & Gas Alliance (June 2025). - A legal challenge to the government's climate plans by Lawyers for Climate Action and the Environmental Law Initiative was heard in the High Court in 2026. ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/environment/589666/government-s-climate-change-plans-go-to-the-high-court)) **Energy** - Announced a government-backed LNG import facility in Taranaki, funded by a levy on electricity of NZ$2–4/MWh (February 2026). **Local government** - With Chris Bishop, proposed abolishing elected regional councils (November 2025). ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/579978/no-more-regional-councils-major-shake-up-of-local-government-announced)) - Gave councils three months to develop amalgamation plans (May 2026). ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/594289/government-gives-councils-amalgamation-ultimatum)) - Ordered a full review of the Dog Control Act after fatal attacks (March 2026). ([RNZ](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/590245/government-orders-complete-review-of-dog-control-act-after-spate-of-attacks)) **Conscience votes** - He was in Parliament for the 2022 conversion-practices vote but was not among the eight National MPs recorded as opposed. ## Controversies - **Climate criticism:** the Greens and climate groups criticised him for leaving the Beyond Oil & Gas Alliance and for the government's climate-policy rollbacks, which are now the subject of litigation (see above). - No personal scandals are recorded in the sources consulted. ## 2026 candidacy - **Electorate:** North Shore - **List ranking:** 13 _Source: candidate questionnaire answers published on [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/national-party), retrieved Oct 2026._ ## Sources - - - - - - - - - - - - - Photo: — Supplied to policy.nz by the candidate/party (Not stated (candidate photo supplied to policy.nz; used for identification))

## Current status

New Zealand First announced Ngatai as its Papakura candidate in July 2026. On 26 August 2026 he stepped down, saying that "after careful consideration" he had decided to step down, after screenshots posted by the social-media account Shubz Live purported to show him discussing a possible run for ACT and being introduced to ACT leader David Seymour and Opportunity leader Qiulae Wong. In a statement he admitted communicating with other parties during "a period of considerable uncertainty about whether I would have the opportunity to stand as a candidate", but said no meetings took place and he made no commitment to another party. Seymour said he remembered getting a message but "did not think it went anywhere". Ngatai said he would continue to support New Zealand First ([RNZ, 26 Aug 2026](https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/politics_election-2026/1136184/nz-first-candidate-steps-down-after-earlier-shopping-himself-around-to-other-parties)).

Because he withdrew before nominations closed, he does not appear on the Electoral Commission's final candidate list (9 October 2026) or on policy.nz, and NZ First has no candidate in [Papakura](../../../../electorates/papakura.md). The Wikipedia candidate list records him as a withdrawn NZ First candidate who had contested Takanini for Vision NZ in 2020 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candidates_in_the_2026_New_Zealand_general_election_by_electorate)).

## Earlier public statements as a candidate

- 17 August 2026: quoted in a NZ First release welcoming the party's commitment to the Mill Road extension in South Auckland ([archived release](../../policies/documents/2026-08-17-new-zealand-first-makes-mill-road-extension-a-priority-for-s.md)).

Standing again in Te Tai Hauāuru in 2026 (Te Pāti Māori is seeking electorate votes only). She stepped back from the campaign in late September 2026 to care for her mother, who died on 21 October 2026. ## Biography Grew up in Pātea and attended New Plymouth Girls' High School; affiliates to Ngāti Ruanui, Ngāti Ruahine, Ngāruahine and Ngā Rauru, with Irish ancestry through her mother. Chief executive of Te Rūnanga o Ngāti Ruanui, which runs health services in Hāwera and Pātea; led Ngāti Ruanui's long legal fight against Trans-Tasman Resources' seabed iron-sand mining off Taranaki (consents ultimately quashed by the Supreme Court). campaigns for Aotearoa as the country's official name and restoring Māori place names. - With Waititi proposed a Parliamentary Commissioner for Te Tiriti with veto powers (2025). ## Controversies - **Treaty Principles Bill haka (November 2024):** named by the Privileges Committee for advancing towards ACT's seats and making a "finger gun" gesture; boycotted the committee, was found in contempt and suspended for 21 days (June 2025). - **MACA Act video (October 2025):** filmed burning a copy of the Marine and Coastal Area amendment law on Parliament's grounds with Tākuta Ferris; Member, Finance and Expenditure Committee | | **Born** | 17 October (year c. 1980), Ōpōtiki | | **2026 election** | contesting Waiariki | | **Wikipedia** | [Rawiri Waititi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rawiri_Waititi) | Photo: Supplied to policy.nz by the candidate/party — [source](https://cdn.sanity.io/images/ubdwo62y/production/3dc9a22391695e7f36b33bd6932ae414b8c6bc3d-1024x1024.jpg) ## Current status Co-leader of Te Pāti Māori (with Debbie Ngarewa-Packer) and MP for **Waiariki** since 2020. Standing again in Waiariki in 2026; Te Pāti Māori is campaigning for electorate votes only (its 2026 list contains only general secretary Lance Norman) and urging supporters to party-vote Labour or Green. In 2025–26 the party went through a bitter internal split that saw MPs Mariameno Kapa-Kingi and Tākuta Ferris expelled (Kapa-Kingi was reinstated by the High Court before forming her own party). ## Biography Rawiri Wikuki Waititi was born in Ōpōtiki on 17 October (c. 1980) and raised at Whangaparāoa near Cape Runaway in Te Whānau-ā-Apanui, attending kōhanga reo and kura kaupapa before moving to West Auckland at 13 (Rutherford High School). Affiliations include Te Whānau-ā-Apanui, Ngāi Tai, Te Whakatōhea, Ngāi Tūhoe, Ngāti Awa, Te Arawa and Ngāti Porou. A fluent te reo speaker, iwi leader, Ringatū minister and kapa haka exponent; grand-nephew of Hoani Waititi. Married to Kiri Tamihere-Waititi (daughter of party president John Tamihere); five children. ## Political career - Labour candidate for Waiariki in 2014 (lost to Te Ururoa Flavell); switched to the Māori Party in 2016. - Won **Waiariki** in 2020 by 836 votes over Labour's Tāmati Coffey, returning the party to Parliament (and bringing in Ngarewa-Packer on the list); confirmed male co-leader on 28 October 2020, replacing John Tamihere. - Re-elected in 2023 with an outright majority (21,500 of 28,958 votes). ## Record & notable actions - Helped negotiate the end of the 2020–21 Waikeria Prison rooftop protest at the inmates' request. - His 2021 refusal to wear a tie ("a colonial noose") led to his ejection and then to Parliament dropping the tie requirement. - Member's bill to remove GST from food (defeated at first reading March 2024, supported only by TPM). - With Ngarewa-Packer proposed a Parliamentary Commissioner for Te Tiriti with a "Tiriti veto" (February 2025); advocates a Māori Parliament, a wealth tax and foreign-policy neutrality ("Switzerland of the South Pacific"). - Voted for the conversion-practices ban (2022) and abortion safe-areas law (2022); against the one-off Queen Elizabeth II Memorial Day holiday (2022). ## Controversies - **Treaty Principles Bill haka (14 November 2024):** with Maipi-Clarke, Ngarewa-Packer and Labour's Peeni Henare performed a protest haka that disrupted the bill's first-reading vote. The three TPM MPs boycotted the Privileges Committee ("kangaroo court"); the committee found them in contempt, and on 5 June 2025 Parliament suspended Waititi for 21 days — the harshest such penalty in its history. An RNZ-Reid Research poll found 54% thought the punishment about right or too lenient, 36% too harsh. - **Suppression breach (August 2023):** suspended for 24 hours for referring to suppressed court proceedings under privilege; the Privileges Committee upheld the action. - Joked at a July 2023 party conference about putting karaka berries in David Seymour's water; Seymour demanded an apology. - Defended the party's 2023 sports-policy wording about Māori "genetic makeup being stronger", later removed from its website, against accusations of racism. - Ejected from the House several times (2021 haka during an argument with Judith Collins; 2023 haka welcoming Meka Whaitiri). - **2025–26 internal conflict:** as co-leader he was at the centre of the dispute in which president John Tamihere accused Kapa-Kingi and Ferris of plotting to replace the leaders; the national council expelled both in November 2025, which Ferris called "plainly unconstitutional". At Waitangi in February 2026 a confrontation with Eru Kapa-Kingi's supporters ended hopes of reconciliation. ## 2026 candidacy - **Electorate:** Waiariki _Source: candidate questionnaire answers published on [policy.nz](https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/te-pati-maori), retrieved Oct 2026._ ## Sources - https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Rawiri_Waititi&oldid=1372456126 - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Te_P%C4%81ti_M%C4%81ori - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candidates_in_the_2026_New_Zealand_general_election_by_electorate - https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/429357/maori-party-s-rawiri-waititi-replaces-john-tamihere-as-co-leader - https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/national/433870/waikeria-prison-unrest-protesters-leave-rooftop-to-meet-waititi - https://e-tangata.co.nz/korero/rawiri-waititi-unapologetically-maori/ - https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/political/556984/te-pati-maori-to-hold-own-hearing-after-boycotting-privileges-committee - https://policy.nz/2026/party-vote/parties/te-pati-maori
